in a walk through the Fylde of North Lancashire from Fleetwood to Garstang last week I was very much struck by the effects produced in the landscape by that gay and attractive though common plant the foxglove. In many situations Nature at times sur- passes the efforts of the gardener in producing bril- liant masses of colour. I saw some patches, which if they had been reproduced by an artist, would be at once condemned as utterly unnatural. A North-East Lancashire correspondent writes :—Owing to the cold and inclement weather in May and the earlier part of June the hay crop in Rossendale threatened:to be an almost complete failure; but subsequent showers and warm weather brought the grass away rapidly, and the farmers are all well satisfied with the crop, which is fully over the average. In Rossendale, owing to the inequalities of the ground and the small size of many of the stone-walled meadows, very few mowing machines are in use in the district, and the grass is chiefly cut by the scythe. Since the commencement of the season there has, as usual, been a great influx of Irish haymaloers into the district. On Tuesday night the weather broke up, and rain fell heavily till early on Wednesday morning, and , during the day the weather was still unsettled. This season, owing to the fine harvest weather, no grass has been sliced in the district. In Rossendale, as elsewhere, scarcely a spray of hawthorn blossom has been seen this year. The buds—like so many of the summer birds— were destroyed by the storm in the second week of May. Even during the recent warm weather only a few stray swallows have been seen, and not a single house martin. These birds, as well as the warblers, were either starved to' death or driven out of the district during the terrible weather in May, and their places have not been taken up by others of the same species. The cuckoos have also' been scarce and mute from the same cause, though a few young and old birds have been recently seen. The star-, hugs are more than usually numerous this year, and , they are increasing rapidly, as the second broods are now ' getting on the wing and are beginning to increase the , already large flocks. From correspondents in various : parts of the North of England and Scotland I hear un- satisfactory accounts of grouse prospects. Everywhere, as in Lancashire, the seasonois expected to be a very poor one; the birds will be few and late, and there will be far too many " cheepers " on the "twelfth." The storm of May occurred at the time when the bulk of the hens were hatching, and the eggs and young were de- tsroyect wholesale.

"SUMMER HOURS."
Sitting in the long grass Weaving daisy chains, Watching dusty hay carts Rolling down the lanes. Soft, delicious odours Mingle with the heat Heavy-headed clover, • Snowy meadow sweet.

"Tip" is lying near me, Idly snapping flies, Rosy tongue out-lolling, Blinking watchful eyes. Swallows skim around us, Laden bees boom past— " Tip" is off in breathless, Hopeless chase at last! tu. Tossing (all unskilful) Faintly scented hay, - 0 the happy hours! 0 the sunny day! Full of song and gladness, Leaving us too soon, • Passing heedless onward, Summer's golden noon!
Cloudlets cluster rosy; Growing shadows creep, And the stately pine tree Rocks the dove to sleep; Phyllis hastens homewards, INodding daisies close Dewy, silken lashes Ereltheir lover goes.

The effect of cotton seed meal upon the milk is to in- crease the cream and ha den the butter. There is no ill- flavour acquired by the butter, as there is with linseed meal, and the colour and texture are better. Professor Stewart recommends salting butter with one-fourth white sugar and three-fourths fine salt (by weight), using one ounce of the mixture for every pound of butter. He says it improves the flavour and keeping quality. If you do not want lumps to form in the cows teats they must be milked out clean and thoroughly squeezed, to dislodge every particle of casein or butter fat which may have adhered together. Careless drying up of cows is file chief cause -of 6lumps and stoppages in the milk ducts.

Ground that has been ,enriched by the applicittion of plenty of farmyard manure is frequently much benefited by the use of lime. Twenty-five bushels of unslaked lime applied once in four or five years works wonders on some soils. Apply it fresn slaked to stubble land atter it has been cleaned and pulverised. Six Shorthorn cows and heifers of the " Sittyton Vic- toria" family were sold recently at Chicago, at prices ranging from £B2 to £172, making the large average of £122 125.; and a " Victoria" bull brought £lOO. In all, Mr. Cummings sold 38 females at an average of £47 Bs., and six bulls averaging £45,165. Webb Brothers' aver- age on 12 bulls was £l6los.jon 51 females £24-ss. A farmer at Cranbrook, in Kent, being unable to ob- tain more than the nominal price of 31s. per quarter for his wheat, decided to have it ground himself. This he did, telling the miller to make the flour as good as pos- sible. The result was that the offal more than paid for , the grinding, and the grower has since been able to sell the whole of the flour at 9d. per gallon, thus realising 425. pit. quarter. Streakiness in butter is a fault which many makers find a difficulty in avoiding. One authority says it is generally caused by using salt after the butter is out of the churn, instead of while it is in the churn. The pro- per time to introduce. the salt is immediately after the butter has "come" in small pieces. Used then, the salt melts, ana the brine salts the butter regularly, and with- out causing streakiness. down quotations for the bulk of the clip this season. - KEEPING MILK SwEE-r.—To keep milk sweet, a York- shire housewife recommends that milk he sealded short of coagulating the casein, which may Ye doae at about 150 degrees Fahrenheit. In large dairies, jacketed or containing convoluted pipes heated by steam are used; thereby avoiding the risk of burning, and so imparting a yozit to the milk. Milk treated in this way will travel well, even in hot weather, and will keep twice as long as ordinary milk. It should, however, be scalded as early as possible after being milked, and it, should be cooled down as rapidly as possible in order to prevent scouring. Another plan is by 'adding antiseptics, or, as they are sometimes called, Milk preservers. - These are carbonate of soda or potash. Glacialine is an article that has found much favour in this country for this purpose. SWEET Sir..kos.—We have recently been asked several times how to make sweet silage. Mr. Fry, who is a great authority on sweet silage, describes his practice of making it as follows :—" Choose a fine day, and in the morning cut sufficient of the crop to be ensiled to cover a foot in depth of the silo. When the crop to be ensiled is trifolium, tares, or similar dense fodder, it is well, if convenient, to begin the silo with one or two cartloads of grass. Allow this to dry in the sun and air until the peculiar sweet smell of hay is distinctly perceptible; this may be the same evening, or not until the next day. Then cart this and spread it lightly on the bottom of the silo. On this lightly and evenly spread more of the fod- der, either dried for a few hours in the sun or mown and carted at once, until the whole is three feet deep. The day after mow and cart direct to the silo sufficient to form a further layer of about three feet. The next day the temperature near the bottom of the silo should be tested,and ought to be at least 90 degrees Fahrenheit. If it be so, put in a further layer of:_three feet; but if

. . not, wait for a day before adding this quantity. The day following an increase of temperature of at least 10 degrees Fahrenheit will be found in the lowest layer; if it reaches 120 degrees Fahrenheit, so much the better. The fermentation will now be well started, and the speed with which the silo may be filled up will ,depend very much upon the nature and condition of the crop. Some judgment is necessary to avoid too much compression of the lower layers of fodder _before the have reached "-

the necessary temperature of 125 degrees Fahrenheit or upwards. In all cases it is preferable to fill the silo too slowly rather than too quickly." TFIE PURCHASING OF FAT CATTLE. Mr. West ley Richards writes to The Times, deelarieg that English farmers lose £5,000,000 or £6,000,000 annually in respect of fat cattle by their imperfect marketing. He refers "to the losses sustained by farmers from the present system of selling cattle by guessing at their weight from their appearance." He says :—" The system gives an unfair advantage to the butcher over the farmer, from the constant opportunities afforded to the former of testing his judgment by the actual carcass weight of every animal he kills. This system of guesswork must, from the nature of the case, take the form of loss to him. Sir John Lawes had -the weight of five fat, Hereford oxen estimated by experts, and the exact carcass weight of each animal ascertained when dead. The difference be- tween the highest and lowest estimate was 192 lbs., or equal to -about 38 lbs. per animal below the actual weight, and it must 'be remeMbered that in this case the estimates of the butchers and experts were not made for a purchase, but for the purpose of seeing how near they could approximate to the real weights. If the estimates had been made for the purpose of purchase in the usual way of business, my experience tells me it would have been from 60 lbs. to 80 lbs. under the actual weight, in- stead of 38 lbs. The only way to reduce to a minimum the risk and uncertainty referred to is to sell on the basis of live weight, subject to the deduction of a percentage for offal—say, 44 per cent. In that way the actual carcass weight of the five animals just mentioned was ascertained to within 9 lbs, or a variation of less than 2 lbs. per animal, which shows the substantial accuracy of weights thus ascertained." Following up this prin- ciple, Mr. Richards has lately applied it "to seven sepa- rate lots, in which fifty-one animals were sold at auc- tions and at Smithfield without reference to weight, at prices ranging from £1 7s. 4d. to £4 is. 6d. per head below the computed value on the basis of live weights. This, taken for the seven lots, was equal to an average loss of £2 ss. sd. per beast; and if applied even at the round figure of £2 per head to the 2,100,000 of fat cattle estimated to he sold in our markets, represents an annual loss of £4,200,000 to the farmers." DRINKS FOR THE lIARvEsr FIELD AND ALL OTHER HARD WORK.—Stokos is the best drink for hard work— ' it is very strengthening, easily made, and cheap. Put a *lb. of oatmeal ground as fine as flaur, about six ounces of loaf sugar, half a lemon cut into slices, into a pan; mix all together with a little warm water, then add a gallon of boiling water; stir thoroughly, and use when cold. The lemon may be omitted, or any other flavour- ing may be used instead. Pure "Lime Fruit Juice" makes an excellent flavouring, about three tablespoon- fuls to the gallon put in when cold. Costs 3d. a gallon. —Cokes is a good nourishing drink, made as follows: 6oz. of sugar, floz. of good fine oatmeal, 4oz. of cocoa, mixed into a thin batter, then add a gallon of boiling water; take to the field in a stone jar. Costs 1-0. a quart.—Lemonade is one of the most refreshing of drinks. It may be made either for present use or to be bottled and mixed with water as wanted. There are many ways of making both kinds. Perhaps the best are :—For pre- sent use—Put 11b. of white sugar, loz. cream of tarter, and two lemons cut in slices (or a teaspoonful of essence of lemon), in a large jug, and pour over all three quarts of boiling water. This is a very cooling drink, and costs about 2d. a quart. For bottling—Dissolve 21b. of lump sugar in a quart of boiling water, add 2oz. of citric acid and two lemons sliced (or a teaspoonful of essence of lemon) ; stir altogether, strain, and bottle when cold. A tablespoonful, more or less, in a glass of water will make a pleasant drink. Cost about is. 3d. a quart bottle, which will make five or six quarts of drinks. Note: One lemon is about equal to 10 drops of essence of lemon, or to 1- drachm of citric acid. If essence of lemon is used in place of lemon it should he mixed in when it is luke- warm.—A good harvest drink i made by boiling koz. hops and koz. of ginger (bruised) in 14- gallons of water for 25 minutes; add 11b. of best brown sugar, and boil ten minutes more • then strain, and bottle while hot; it will be ready for drinking when cold. It should be kept in a cool place. Dried horehound may be used instead of hops. Cost 3d. a gallon.—Ginger beer may be made by pouring 2 gallons of boiling water over 11b. of lump sugar, loz. of bruised ginger, and two lemons sliced (or 20 drops of essence of lemon) ; when lukewarm, add one tablespoonful of barm ' - let it stand 12 hours, then bottle it. It will be ready for use in 24 hours. Cost 4d. a gallon.—An agreeable drink is made by pouring half-a- - pint of boiling water on a teaspoonful of marmalade. Stir well.—Boiling water poured on a few slices of lemon, with a little sugar, makes a very refreshing drink.—lt is quite a mistake to suppose that beer or spirits give strength. They do give a spurt to a man, but that quickly goes off, and spurts, in hard, heavy work, too often made, certainly lessen the working powers. Bring with thee airs from heaven, or blasts from hell, Be thy ihtents wicked or charitable. Thou comest in such a Questionable shape, That I will speak to thee. —Bltak.espere. Many years ago when it was vile custom for ghouls in human form, yclept " resurrectioniats," to visit chnrch-yards in the dead hoar of night in order to despoil the graves of their contents for the purpotte of supplying doctors with "subjects" to operate upon, there resiaed in a village which I need not here particularise, an eccentric old man who was knowa throughout the neighbourhood as Billy-o'-Tum's. It must not for a moment be supposed that Billy was in any way lacking in the qaalities essential to a due regard to looking to the main chance—nothing of the kind. Billy could drive a bargain with anyone, and in such a manner that he generally ceme off with the advantages all in his favour. It would have puzzled a Kentucky lawyer to have given a definite idea of Billy's "profession," or how he managed to procure the means of livelihood sufficient to supply him with his modest wants. He might be truly termed an ail-round man, and so was rarely out of employ- ment for long together by one or other of the local employers of labour. One evening as Billy was trudging along a country lane, just outside the Village where he lived, be was somewhat astonished to come across a couple of rough-looking fellows who were bending beneath the weight of something which was enclosed in a large sack. " Hello !" ejaculated our friend to himself, "some o' thoose rascally body snatchers aw reckon?" The men eyed him rather suspiciously as they passed him; but Billy's simple appearance apparently gave tbem no alarm as, whistling a lively tune, they bore their burden along. "Aw expect," solikquised Billy, " thur makin thur way to owd doctor —'s, an, if 80, au'il follow um to see heaw they go on." By going another road Billy managed to reach the doctor's residence just as the two mi-n were some yards from the garden gate which led to the back entrance of the doctor's house. Hiding himself beyond the friendly shelter of a hedge close by, Billy watched the men carry the sack to the back door. some hitch, however, must have occurred in the arrangements' for directly afte wards the men re-apppared with the sack and is contents, and, cursing fearfully at their evident non-success to effect a bargain, left the place. " Thur's sianialut wrung between um au' th' doctor," said Billy, as he watched them retrace their way down the lane. "Happen they'n axt too mich brass. Chus heaw it is au 11 follow um an' see whetr they tak th' corpse to; fur that it is one aw dust bet ml Sunday clooas." So saying he cau- tiously followed the two men until they arrived at an empty house on the outskirts of the village. Here they paused, and, placing the sack upon the ground, looked carefully to the right and left of the road, in order, no doubt, to make sure they were alone. Apparently satisfied with their sur- vey they lifted the sack and carried it into the cellar, where, having left it where they were sure it would be safe from molestation until their return, they emerged from the place, and turned their steps in the direction of the village. Having made sure that the coast was clear, Billy hurried off to the doctor, whom he was fortunate enough to find at home.

In answer to his knock, Billy was told to come in. . "Well, Billy," said the man of medicine. "what is the matter now ?" "Am aw reet, doctor," said our hero, "in sayin that that wur a what yo co'n a subject ut thoose two men browt yo a while alto ?" The doctor, knowing that his visitor's secreay was to be depended on, unhesitatingly answered in the affirmative. "Aw thowt as mitch, rueetur; but wurn't it up to th' mark, or what, as they took it away agen ?" " Well, Billy, I may tell you it was as good a subject as ever I saw, but, unfortunately, the price they asked for it was above my meths." "Oh, aw see. Neaw doctor," with a merry twinkle in his eyes—"aw think aw con manage to let yo ha' that theer corpse a greight deeul chepper then they'n °Sart it if yo'n a mind." , "Can you! Well, Billy, I don't mind paying a'reason- I able sum of money; but I certainly could not afford to give anything like the price asked for by the men who have recently been here." " Heaw mich win yo' gimme, doctor ?" The doctor named a certain sum which appeared highly satisfactory to Billy, who directly afterwards took his leave. Billy chuckled with inward satisfaction as he went on his way; for a scheme had entered his brain which would not only procure him his reward but enable him to have a joke at the expense of the two resurrectionists. " Aw'll play um aich a marlock as 'll atop urn fro' comin' this road agen fer some time to come," said Billy, "see if aw dunno!" Late that same night Billy proceeded to the cellar in which lay the corpse. He listened intently for a few seconds in order to make sure that no one was about. Nothing disturbing the solemn stillnesa of the night he pre- pared to descend into the cellar, which he did in a manner that he had not at all calculated upon; for, unaware that the second step was missing, he over-balanceel himself, falling with a loud thud against the door at the bottom! For a moment he lay stunned, his head having made a violent though unsuccessful effort to force its way through one of the panels of the door. Never had our hero more cause than at that moment to rejoicr) in possessing a thick- ness of skull that could not be matched in all the village. Rubbing a lump the size of a goose egg which had arisen an the side of his cranium, Billy gathered himself together, and after making sure that all was quiet within and without, tried the dory:, which, being only latched, yielded to his touch. I mrec not omit to mention that Billy bad provided himself with a dark lantern, by means of which he was en- abled to pick his way to where the sack reposed. "By gum !" soliloquised our hero, gazing occasionally in an uneasy manner around the cellar, "it's a god job aw danno' beleeav in ghosts, or else aw shudno' like to tackle th' wark aveve getten in bond. Neaw for it!" and so say- in.. he exerted all his strength to drag the corpse out of the sack. This being accomplished he carried the body in his arms out of the cellar into the empty house, where he left It hr the time being Re-entering the cellar he, in accord- ance with the plot he had formed, ensconced himself in the sack, truging to his usual good luck to carry him safely through his adventure. For nearly an hour Billy lay in his unenviable position, and had it not been that he could not resist the desire to terrify the body•snatchers so that they would not dare to come that way again, he would have left the place and carried away the corpse at the next convenient opportunity. " Nawe," he soliloquised, "aw'll face it eawt neaw, chin what comes or goes." Jost as the midnight hour was striking from the old parish church clock, footsteps were heard by the sacked one de- scending the cellar steps. NCAW for it," said Billy to himself, and stretching him- self out to his full length, he preoared to await the advent of the two rascals who at this uncanny hour had come to remove their property. Having cautiously peeped through the doorway, in order to prevent a surprise should anybody be lying in wait for them, they, sati.fied with their scrutiny, passed in. Utterly unsuspicious that the sack contained a "live corpse "as Pat would say, they liffed the sack up and carried it between th,im out of the cellar into the road. It required all the presence of mind Billy possessed to refrain from uttering a yell of pain when, on reaching the top of the cellar, the men let the sack slip from their grasp where it fell upon the hard stones in such a way as to add to another lump to the one already resting upon Billy's head. Lifting the sack shoulder high, the men proceeded along the lane until they came to a large track of MOM land. Suddenly the men were startled to bear a voice from the interior of the sack say in a sepulchral tone: " Aw wondlpir heaw mich th' doctor 'll gie yo for mi when yo getten mi theer ?" With a combined yell of fear the men hurriedly dropped the sack, and ran as though the evil one himself were at their very heels. Their hats flew off—borne by the wind in the direction of the "corpse "—but such trivial matters were not of sufficient importance to arrest their headlong career. When certain that he was free to leave the sack, Billy did so; and, having secured the two hats he, with a chuckle of delight hurried home, confident that the real corpse would not be disturbed until he chose to go for it. Suffice it to say the village doctor got his" subject," and a merry laugh had they at the clever manner in which Billy had outwitted the resurrectionists who, our readers may be cere an, were never again seen in the neighbourhood. —J. The present Pope is a gentleman with a keen sense of humour. Accredited to the Papal court is a functionary who: represents the political interest of four Central American republics, and who is already bedizened with the stars of almost every order created by the Pontificate. Not long ago a fresh negotiation was concluded satisfac- torily to the Mother Church, and the custom of b(-riving a new distinction required to be kept up, but how to do it perplexed the Papal chamberlain. On application in the emergency to Leo himself, the latter said, "This time give him a snuff-box with my portrait." The diplomatist accepted the golden gift, detached the portrait there- from, and appeared at the next audience with it hanging from his neck. Another State negotiation unexpectedly arose, and when it was solved again there came up the question of an honorarium. "This tie," said Leo, "give him a marble statue, and see if hewill wear that around his neck."

"SAVE HIM FIRST."—Some years ago there was an ac- cident in a coal mine near Baton, in gloucestershire. Six men were going down into the mine, when the people at the top heard of the accident, and handle of the cart in which they were sitting broke, and they were all killed. A man and a boy had been cling- ing to the rope which held the cart, and as the accident happened they each made a spring, and managed i to catch hold of a long iron chain which is always hung down the side of a coalpit as a guide. When the ple found that someone was clinging to the chain, they sent down a man to rescue him. The man himself was securely fastened to the end of a rope, and had another noose or loop of rope which he could tie round the body of the man to be rescued, and then they would both be drawn up together. He came first to the boy Daniel HaOing, and was just going to seize him, when the boy cried, "Don't mind me; I can still hold on a little; but Joseph Brown, who is a little lower down, is nearly exhausted. save him first." So the.brave lad hung on patiently for another quarter of an hour, and saved his friend's life at the risk of his own. div.head: COTTA GE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTA GE GARDENING.

To all like ourselves who had autumn and winter vegetables to transplant, the rain that has fallen this week must have been most acceptable, as with the arid atmosphere and scorching sun, it was useless removing , anything that was expected to grow. All such crops • should be now in their permanent quarters or they will be of little use, and as we have often witnessed their destiny will be the rubbish heap instead of the boiling pot. Gardens composed of poor soil or that which is cold and stiff require the planting to be done much earlier than those that are rich and naturally warm. Lettuce: Successional sowings may be made of these, and if space permits sow where they are to stand either broad cast or in shallow drills, and thin out the neces- sary distance as soon as the plants are large enough. Transplanting is always attended with more or less check, and every advantage should be taken to escape it. Lettuce suffer from this operation more than any plant, and after the expenditure of much labour in watering with the view of re-establishing them, the plants oftener than not run up, and for our pains we have had a number of tough blueish leaves clothing a lanky stem, instead of a head white, crisp, and tender. The fact is you never know how they are likely to turn out after they are transplanted, and those who grow for exhibition should never attempt it, but adopt instead the shallow drill method, and sow every fortnight or three weeks a yard or two of length each time. Some will then certainly be at their best on the day of the show, and no more ground will be occupied by the crop than is taken up in the usual way. Celery: Advancing crops of this should have liberal supplies of manure water, regardless of the rainfall. Horse or cow manure placed in a tub of water well stirred and allowed to settle will admirably answer the purpose. Soot may also be added to them, and the quantity is of not much im- portance as we only take as much of the liquid as will well colour the water used in watering at first, and in- crease the strength as we go on. If the manure and soot are good, this is a strong stimulant, and it must not be confounded with the contents of the ordinary cess- pool, which may have stronger odour and darker colour. Scarlet runner beans should have some kind of support, and the cheapest and best we are acquainted with are nets manufactured for the purpose. We have used one for six seasons, and it is likely to last another year or two. For small gardens, however, it is best to sow a few in a circle here and there, and insert a stout pole, 6ft. to Bft. high, in the citatre, and fasten strong strings from its summit to stuTnps firmly fixed in the ground, so that when these are covered with the bean growth the whole will have the appearance of a tent. All to whom we have recommended this plan have been highly pleased with the result. , THE FRONT GARDEN.—Road-side front gardens had a deplorable appearance before the rain came to wash I away the dust that had collected on flowers and foliage. Some owners of gardens never allow them to get very bad, and they persevere in keeping them clean by wash- ing some or all of the plants every evening with the syringe or watering pot, with spreader held well up above the plants, to give some force to the water. This is best done in the evening, so that it may act as a dewing to the plants, and in windy weather it is as well to dispense with artificial water, as the dust is blown on the wet foliage, and adheres to it much worse than when dry. Delphiniums (Larkspurs) are splendid objects in a mixed garden, and one is astonished that plants having so many excellent qualities should be so rarely seen in front gardens. The plume-like flower ',stems may be tied to stakes, or if their height should be an objection, they may be pegged down within six inches or a foot of the surface of the ground, and the numerous flowering side branches may be staked and a grand effect produced. They thrive best in good, deep, moderately moist soil; but they do well in most soils, and are perfectly hardy. Should they at any time show symptoms of debility, an early opportunity should be taken to move them, if only a foot or two from where they are. Before replanting mix some good manure with the soil, and if the latter is light, water and mulch them in dry weather. The plants are propagated by dividing the roots just as they com- mence to grow in spring, and as this is the best period to transplant, it offers an excellent opportunity to take pieces off to increase the stock and secure healthy vigorous growth. Seeds may also be sown in the open ground in April or May on a friable bed in a warm posi- tion; but as they are so liable to be destroyed by slugs, it is better to sow in pans, which is the plan adopted by Mr. Miller, of Woodplumpton" whose strain of this beau- tiful class of plants is probably unrivalled, in Lancashire, at any rate. THE WlNDOW.—Pelargoniums should be turned out of doors to mature their wood, as they go out of flower, and the water supply must be gradually reduced. Double Geraniums are best indoors in showery weather, as the wet lodges between the thickly-set florets and brings on decay. Plants that have got one-sided through being in the window a long time should have the naked side turned to the sun by degrees, and if placed out of doors they soon come round into a respectable shape. Fuchsias and Balsams should not be potted after this date. If they are required for exhibition, continue to pick off the flowers, as it is useless to have any expand more than ten days before the show, for they will drop off ere they reach the show-ground.

Large hands threaten Ningyan'town The Commissioner of the district recently informed the rzaders in Ningyan that, owing to the smallness of the force at his disposal and the fact that the troops were being over- Worked, no men "Pre available to protect the town. He recommended that all valuables should be sent into the fort. The insurgents have unsuccessfally.attacked two fortified pests near Ningvan. There has been much desultory fiAht- ,g in this district, the result being generally unsatisfac-

tory. CALCUTTA. SUNDAY —Two new police levies are to be raised in India. and IVO trained policemen are to be sent Ur service in Upper Burmah. ENGLAND AND RUSSIA IN CENTRAL ASIA. SurrA, MONDAY.—A eilif,reace has arisen between the British and Russian members of the Afghan boundary Com- mission concerning the locality of liw-iza S der. The Rue- tians contend that the poet of that name mentioned in the agreement of 1873 as upon the frontier is in reality situated twelve mile! above the present fondly recognised frontier hie. The Eoglish members of the Commission refuse to accept this contention, one consequently the claim has been referred by the Commissioners to their respective Goyera- __

MONDAY—The panic in commercial circles caused by the proposed scheme for the construction of a harbour at Damietta continues, and the construction of new buildings has been discontinued. An influential depntition waited upon the Khedive to-day, and presented a monster Petition to His Highness expressing disapproval of the scheme. The Khedive. in reply, said that he should always Inde4vour to promote the prosperity of Alexandria, adding that nothing would be decided until the prop .sal had been Minutely examined. Meanwhile he desired that the con- Struetion of new buildings should be continued, in order to Prevent the distress which would otherwise be caused among the workmen OPENING OF VIE SERVIAN PARLIAMENT. Niscs, MoNney.—The Skuptschina was opened to-day by King Milan. who, in his Speech from the Throne, thanked the Servian people and the army for the sacrifices Which they made during the late war. His Majesty laid areas on the fact that the relations between Servia and Bul- garia were the same as before the outbreak of the late war, and this passage of the speech was received with loud cheers by the House.

THE CHOLERA. Rolm SATURDAY —The returns of the cholera in the Province of B•indisi for the past 24 hours show a further abatement in the severity of the disease, there having been 47 cases and 31 deaths, against 75 cases and 44 deaths on the preceding day. ROTIE, SUNDAY.—The cholera returns for the last 24 hours report seven cases and two deaths in the town of Brindisi; 16 cases and two deaths at Fracavilla Fontana ; eight cases and five deaths at Latieno ; two cam at San Vibe ; two cases et One ; four cases and two deaths at SAn Donaci ; and two cases at Codigoro. No cases are announced from Venice. TRIESTE, WRDNESDAY.—Five cases of cholera and one death have occurred here during the last 24 hours. Fevers, WEDNB,DAY.—Since the outbreak of the epidemic there have been 94 cases of cholera and 55 deaths here. During the last 24 hours two deaths have occurred. Roam, WEDKRSDAY —The cholera returns for the past 24 hours report 9 cases and 2 deaths in the town of Brindisi, 14 cases and 2 deatt-s at Francavilla Fontana, 7 cases and 2 deaths at Seri Vito Normanni,3 cases and 2 deaths at Lotine, and 3 cases and no deaths at Ostuni. No cases or deaths secured at Venice. DISTURBANCES IN NEW ZEALAND. WeemsereoN. MONDAY.—A vrious. datturbance has °c- acted near Hapra. Five hundred Maori men and women made an incursion on some lands belonging to Europeans and commenced ploughing and erecting a 'where." The police arrested several chiefs, including Titokowaru. After a slight resistance the other Meoris were dispersed. Fur- ther troubles were expect.d. The Government has ordered the arrest oft the Maori chief, Te Whiti, as the instigator of the raid. GERM IN TRADE AND THE EAST. Binterre, MONDAY. Another proof of the energy with which the Germans are pushing their foreign trade is seen in the transmission home by the Cease at Canton of a col- lection of samotes of foreign goods sold in the Chinese mar- kets. The collection has come to Gotha, and it will be placed at the service. of manufacturers exporting to the East. It is stated that Dr. Peters, the president of the German African Company, who has lately had an interview with H. M. Stanley; entertaies the hope of constructing a railway from Deres-Selaam into the interior of East Africa with the aid of English ca ,ital. THE CANADIAN FISHERIES QUESTION. ' HALIFAX, MONDAY- Judgmcnt was delivered to-day by the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia in the action brought against the master of the American fishing vessel David J. Adams, which was seized by the Canadian authorities in May last for buying bait in iiihy 3arbour. The Court imposed the full p-tealty with costs, for violation of the Act of 59 George 111., cap. 38, by entering the Annapolis basin for illegal purposes. The case was undefended, the captain admitting th, infringement of the law as master of the vessel. SATURDAY.—After six days' travelling, the Pre- mier and Lady Maedonald have reachei this place, having travelled over 2,000 miles by rail, and having visited South- ern Manitobia, and made a stay of two days at Winnipeg. Sir John received many addresses ef welcome, and at all the stations on the line his arrival was awaited by crowds, to whom he made addresses. VANCOUVER AGAIN DESTROYED BY FIRE. NEW YORE, wATCrIIDAY —Another most destructive fire has occurred at Vanc iuver, British Columbia. which is re- presented as again in *ghee. Toe telegraph office has been burned, and no details have vet been received. ATTEMP "ED REVOLUTION IN MEXICO. NEW YORK, SUNDAY —AIiViC S received here from Mexi- co state that the revolutioa is's are now making raids on the ranches. It is moreover declared that the insurrectionary movement is increasing in the State of Tamaulipa and Spreading to that of Nuevo Leon. The whole of the dis- affected region is in arms. •TURBANCES IN YASSIN. SPINAGAR, SUNDAY I oekhart, who has arrived at Chitral, by way of 13 arlakshan, accompanied by four Europeans, reports that disturbances have occurred in the Yassin territory. An attack was made on Yassin by Mulka- man, a pretender to the Yassin chieftainship. He was,how- ever, repelsed,l7 of his followers being killeel. Mulkatnan, who had been taking refuge in Tenger, is the elder brother Of Pehlwan, who was dispossessed of Yassin by the present ruler of Chitral. Pehl wan, who had killed his own brother, Mefwali, notorious as tl-azt murderer of Mr. Hayward, was afterwards assassinated by Mulkaman. SERDUS RIOTING AT MARSEILLES. TUESDLY —There were renewed and more serious disturbances at Marseilles on Al wday night. A great crowd attacked the officeas of the Rtyalist newspapers and the gendarmerie had to he called out to prevent their be- ing sacked. There was a deeermin,rl fight, several of the police and eoldiers being wounded. There were numerous arrests.

PORTUGAL AND THE VATICAN. ROME, WEDNESDAS.—The diff,rences between Portugal and the Holy Sea concerning the jurisdiction of the Arch- bishop of Goa having been seltl.d, the Vatican has drawn up a plan for the esNblishtnent of a Catholic hierarchy in the East Indies. The Pope to-day examined the Pro- posal, which will shortly be communicated to the British 7ment.

YOW WILL KNOW! —Advt A traveller, lately describing a tropical shower, wrote to a friend in the tellowing words :—" The raindrops were extremely large, varying in size from a shilling to eighteenpence." • "Step this way, if you please, ladies," said the gracious Poor walker, as he led of with a majestic wave of his hand. "We are sorry," said a lady, "but we never learned to step that way." Benevolent old Lady (who has just given a penny to a small rustic) : Now, my dear, what do you say ?—Small Rustic (with native politneness) : Give us another ! Collapse of old lady. A clergyman who married four couples in one hour the other day remarked to a friend that it was "pretty fast work." "Not so very fast," respoOed his friend; "it's only four knots an hour." TEE LORD OF 131111011LEY.—The story of the romantic marriage of the Lord of 13urghley,the subject of Tennyson's famous poem, is thus recorded. In the year 1791, Henry Cecil, then a man of seven or eight and thirty, nephew and heir to the Earl of Exeter and Lord of Burghley of those days, came to live in the quiet village of Bolas, on the banks of the river Tern, in a remote corner of Shrop- shire. While young he had been led into a marriage which had proved unhappy, and when he came to Shrop- shire had recently divorced his wife. In a melancholy mood he resolved to hide himself from the world, and, concealing his birth and rank, he assumed the name of Jones and the profession of a travelling artist, and lodged during some months in the house of a farmer called Thomas Hogging. Here he fell in love with the farmer's fair young daughter, Sarah, and, with her parents' con- sent, made her his wife. The names of the contracting parties may still be read in the parish register of the Shropshire village where the wedding took place on the 3rd of October, 1791. Upon his uncle's death, a year afterwards, Mr. Cecil succeeded to the earldom ; and without telling his secret he brought his bride home to Burghley, where she learned it for the first time. div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JULY 24. 1886
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JULY 24. 1886

THE GENERAL ELECTION. The Clonmei Town Council have decided to change the name of the principal street in Clonmel (John- ston-street) to "Gladstone-St.," M recognition of Mr. Gladstone's services to Ireland. Mr. Tasker Toler, of London, has issued an ad- dress ns a Unionist candidate. The candidature of Mr. Ferguson, of Novars, as a Giadstonian, is re- ceived with much favour by the advanced Liberals in the constituency. On Saturday, on behalf of Mr. Justin McCarthy, a petition was lodged in the Common Pleas Office, Dublin, against Mr. Lewis's return as a member of Parliament for Derry City, on the grounds of alleged personation, bribery, and intimidation. Parliament meets on Thursday week. The swear- ing-in of members and the . election of Speaker will constitute the first week's business, the re-elections ; will occupy another week, and it is probable, there- fore, that no legislative business will be undertaken before about August 19th. Mr. Gladstone states, in a letter which has been received at Leith, that he has decided to it in the House of Commons for Midlothian. At a meeting of Liberal Unionists of Leith on Wednesday even- ing it was decided to invite Sir George Trevelyan to become a candidate for the representation of the

burghs. The Liberals of North Lonsdale are considering the advisability of presenting a petition against the return of Mr. W. G. Ainslie, the successful Conser- vative candidate. Evidence is being collected, and it is alleged that cases of intimidation, hiring of licensed carriages, and other illegal practices can be substantiated. During the polling for South Tyrone, on Satur- day, a serious disturbance took place at Aucihna- cloy. A number of persons received injuries from bludgeons, and the police were for some time povverless, but eventually managed to make a num- ber of arrests. A large 'force of extra police was telegraphed for, and in the evening all was quiet. " Barrister" writes:—l have read without any I feelings of surprise the accounts of the riots at Bel- fast. Lord R. Churchill is no doubt quite satisfied I with the results of his recommendation to Ulster ."Ulster will fight. Ulster will be right." Ulster has fought, and it will be for the nation at large to say, not whether Ulster was right in :•() doing, but whether a person who has held the office of Cabinet. Minister "was right" in recommending it to do so. Mr. Henry Broadhurst, M.P., addr:ssing his con- stituents at Nottingham on Monday night, said it I"was popularly supposed that the Liberal party was defeated in the country. Ile owned it was so in one sense. Mr. Gladstone had been defeated on one question, and on one question only, but many of those who were to-day counted among his oppo- nents in the House of Commons were with him nearly the whole way on the question. They had no reason to regret having had the present election, notwithstanding its results, for the Liberal party had been purified. He thought they would again see the whole army of Liberalism rallying round the standard of their old commander. An informal gathering of members of the Cabinet, the first since Mr. Gladstone's return to London, took place at Downing-street on Saturday night, when the Premier entertained his colleagues at dinner. The only Minister unable to attend was Lord Granville, who is still suffering from the effects of his recent illness. A free interchange of views took place in regard to the events of the last few weeks and the future attitude of Home Rile Liberals, and it is reported that tolerable unanimity prevailed as to the inexpediency of delay in acknol,v- ledging the defeat of the Government. As a result, it is believed that immediate resignation will take place. The Press Association has reason to believe that Lord Hartington has been sounded as to his willingness to co-operate with Lord Salisbury in the formation of a new Cainet, bat has declined. Under these circumstances there is no doubt that Mr. Gladstone's successor will be Lord Salisbury, and that the incoming administration will be eon- servative pure and simple. In reply to a letter from Mr. J. W. Dtinford, of Hackney, asking the Rev. Stephen Gladstone whether it was true "that periodically he received the visits of Romish priests to instruct him in their doctrines, and that he had a confessional box at. Hawarden Church in continual use," he has sent the following :—" Hawarden Rectory, Chester, July 18. Dear sir,—You say a friend has given up Mr. Gladstone and his cause because he knows as a fact. that lam a ROMatliSt in disguise. I can only say that he must be more foolish to believe this than even to change his political view for such a reason.

If I were so, I should be a monster. To eat the bread of the Church of England and to be a traitor all the while is so good as not to be worth a denial. But for your sake I will say I have never faltered in my attachment to that church, and it is wholly unlikely that I ever shall falter. There never has been any confessional box in this church to my knowledge, and I certainly have not the slightest desire to have one. Neither has any Romish priest ever been here to teach me anything. I simply seek to carry out the church's instructions to me in re- gard to my public and private ministrations. If you will take a word of advice from me, it is never to believe a single tale related in the Tory papers about Mr. Gladstone or anyone immediately related to him. His long life and labours will bear him a brave witness.—Yours very faithfully (signed), STEPHEN E. GLADSTONE." RESIGNATION OF THE GOVERNMENT RESOLVED UPON. A Cabinet Council was held on Tuesday afternoon at Mr. Gladstone's official residence, Downing-Street, London. The object of the meeting was to decide what course the Ministry should adopt consequent upon the result of the General Election. As was anticipated, the Government decided to resign

forth kith. The announcement that a Cabinet Council was to be held drew a large crowd of people together in the neighbourhood of the Treasury at noon, and between that time and one o'clock the crowd be- came largely augmented, the impression being that the Council was to meet at twelve. The hour, how- ever, was two o'clock, and the crowd remained in Downing-street Until that time. Mr. Gladstone had been engaged indoors all the morning. Mr. Stansfeld was the first Minister who reached Down- ing-street, walking over from the Local Government Board Offices. The Marquis of Ripon walked from the Admiralty, and his Lordship was followed by Mr. Mundella, who came from the Board of Trade Offices. A cab afterwards arrived from Carlton House Terrace, containing a wheeled chair, into which Earl Granville, on his arrival a few minutes afterwards, was lifted from his carriage. Lord Rosebery, who arrived about the same time, assisted Earl Granville's servants to carry his lordship in. Lord Rosebery was loudly cheered by the crowd. Lord Kimberley next arrived, and Mr. Campbell- Bannerman drove up after him. Earl Spencer and Mr. Morley followed, amidst much cheering from the spectators. The Lord Chancellor was the next arrival. Mi. Childers was the last to arrive, and all the Ministers were then present. The Central News says :—A large number of mem- bers of Parliament are already in town in anticipa- tion. The political clubs were crowded on Tuesday, and there was everywhere considerable speculation at the probable composition of the new Cabinet. At the Carleton Club, where there was a large attend- ance, much satisfaction was expressed at the an- nouncement that Lord Salisbury would return to London immediately. It was generally assumed at the Conservative headquarters that the new Ad- ministration will differ considerably in its compo- sition from that over which Lord Salisbury last pre- sided. No importance was attached to a report that Mr. W. H. Smith will be the new Chief Secre- tary for Ireland, the general belief being that the right hon. gentleman will go to the Upper House, and that the post in question will be offered to Mr. Edward Stanhope. Amongst the appointments assumed at the Carlton to be certain were Lord R. Churchill to the India Office, Lord llalsbury to the Lord Chancellorship, Lord Ashbourne to the Irish Lord Chancellorship, and Sir M. H. Beach to the Ex- chequer. It is understood that Lord Carnarvon does not desire to re-enter the Cabinet, and Lord Har- rowbST, who held the Privy Seal last year, is not in good health, and it is believed will decline to take office. Room will probably be made in the new Ad- ministration for Mr. Edward Clarke, but it is taken for granted that Sir R. Webster be again Attor- ney-General, and that Mr. H. Macdonald will be Lord-Advocate for Scotland. Mr. Davitt has cabled a reply to the Irish World's recent article advocating obstruction to all legisla- tion beneficial to the English masses. "This," he says, "would be a suicidal proceeding. The strug- gle for Irish liberty ought to be run parallel with thorough friendliness towards the aspirations of the British democracy for better social existence and earnest efforts for securing true economic freedom in field, workshop, and everywhere. The policy you are credited with advocating would, if carried out, play the game of the aristocracy against this country and the British masses, and lose Ireland the sympathy and support of a million and a half of voters in Great Britain." LORD SALISBURY SENT FOR BY THE QUEEN. At the Carlton Club Mr. Stanhope is spoken of in connection with the Irish Secretaryship, and amongst the gentlemen who held subordinate posts in the last Conservative Administration, Baron Henry de Worms is looked upon as likely to obtain promotion to Cabinet rank. But, of course, until Lord Salisbury has had an interview with Her Majesty, and has consulted with his leading co- adjutors, his views on the subject will not become known. At Downing-street, and in most of the other Go- vernment offices, preparations are being made by Ministers for an early departure. Mr. Gladstone was busy during Wednesday arranging his papers and books, and Lord Dalhousie's effects are already in process of removal from the Scotch Office. The special messenger who left Downing-street for Osborne on Tuesday returned to London on Wednesday, reaching Downing-street at two o'clock. The Royal message was at once communicated to the members of the Cabinet, most of whom were at their respective offices prOparing for'their early de- parture from Whitehall. The Queen's message to Lord Salisbury was tele- graphed from Osborne to his lordship at Auvergne, and it is expected that the Marquis will proceed direct to the Isle of Wight. Lord Salisbury in his telegram, received in London on Wednesday after- noon, simply stated that he would be in the me- tropolis on Friday afternoon. According to present arrangements Mr. Gladstone will not go down to Osborne until the new Cabinet is ready to take office, when all the retiring Minis- ters will pay the usual formal visit to the Queen to deliver up the seals of office, and on the same day their successors will have atadience of Her Majesty for the purpose of kissing hands on their appoint- ment. A special journey to Osborne by Mr. Glad- stone has been rendered unnecessary by the fact that the right hon. gentleman in his written com- munication to the Queen, sent on Tuesday, ex- plained fully the reasons for the decision of the Cabinet, and for his recommendation that Lord Sal- isbury should be sent for It is now officially stated that the Queen has been pleased to accept the resignation of the Ministry, and that her Majesty has commanded the attend- ance of Lord Salisbury at Osborne to receive her Majesty's commands.

F,RAL NEWS.

The Annual Assembly of the United Methodist Free Church next year will be hod at Louth. At the sitting of the Wt•sleydn Couference on Wednesday, it was decided to bold the ntxr Cpnference in Manchester.

It is proposed to hold a Jubilee Exhibition at Giasgow, towards which several trauesmen have started a guarantee fund. Maria Van Z tat, the American opera singer, has been stricken wito a bad form cf paralysis. She is only 24 years of age. A man named Ge3rge Barns died at Belfast on Thursday from the elf -et of a gunshot wound received daring the riots on the 13th inst. The Paris "Figaro "states that the Ckinese Government has decided to apply to the F,rench engineers for the early construction of railways in China. An engine ran into a passenger train at the Exchange Station, Liverpool, on Thursday evening, and three persons were injured, one of them very seriously. At Monmouth Assizes, on Saturday, Thomas Flavell Was found guilty of the manslaughter of his wife at Newport, on May 27th, and was sentenced to peeal servitude for life. The minors connected with the Treorky and Tretierbert collieries, who had been out on strike for some time, returned to work on sei,dnesday on the emp!oyers' terms, namely, a. raiuction of o3d per ton. The besinees of the Manchester Assizes was continued on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Cave. Two prisoners charged with stealing money were acquitted, and a case of alleged fraud was par, ly heard. It has been decided at the War Office to promote the for- mation of a corps of volunteer submarine miners, to co-oper- ate with the Royal Engineers for the defence of certain commercial ports of the United Kingdom. The Leicestershire Cup Stakes tell to the favourite on !Wednesday, Lord Hosting's Melton winning cleverly, carrying the top weight of 9st. 41b. Mr. Jennings'a Exmoor was second, and Prince Soltykoff's Wise Child third _

A reduction of 21- per cent. in the wages rite fr the colliers in the Rhondda Valley was on Monday an- nounced, the reduction, according to the sliding, scale, to last three months. Much distress, it is said, exists in the district.

KILLED BY BEIPS.—At Ludlow, on Tuesday evening, Mr. John Adnev, a former Mayor of that place, was in his gar- d,ll attending to his bees when they attacked ana swarmed upon him, stinging him so severely that he died before medical assistance arrived. .

A SOLICITOR SENTENCED TO PENAL SERVITCDE.---At Manchester Assizes, on Tuesday, Alfred Outrarn, solicitor, was sentenced to ten yearb' penal servitude, and Samuel Kil- patrick, builder, to seven years, for arson with intesit to de- fraud the Western Insurance Company. RAID ON A NIHILIST MEETING.—A secret meeting of Nihilists was surprised by the police at Warsaw the other night. An encounter ensued on the appearance of the officers, and two detcctives were killtd. Numerous arrests have been made in connection with the affair. A TERRIBLE DEATH.—At Woolwich Arsenal, on Saturday afternoon, Daniel Moriarty became immersed in about eight 1 tons of st!el. prepared in connection with the construction of part of the 68-ton gun. With great difficulty a small portion of the remains was rescued for the purpose of the inquest. In consequence of half-holiday, sufficient time had I not been allowed for the cooling of the metal. SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT AN IRONWORKS.—On Monday morning a shocking accident occurrLd at tbe Mossbay Iron- works at Workington, resulting in the death of one man and the injuring of another so seriously that it is thought im- possible be csn recover. The accident occurred near tire Ilarge boiler' one of the valves bursting, and the men were dreadfully scalded. The man who was injured bas been taken to Whitt-haven Infirmary.

TRAGIC SIIICIDE OF Ale OCTOGENARIAN.—A tragic sui- cide was reported on Tuesday from Pembroke, South Wales, where the lifeless body of Mr. John Merriman, aged 82 years, has been found on the pavement in the street. The deceased, who formerly carried on an extensive iron foundry in the town, had cut his throat with a razer, and afterward, fell from his bedroom to the pavement below. He bad been much troubled in mind, and had delusions at times. THE BELFAST RIOTS.— At Downpatrick Assizes, On Saturday, the case against Norman Pirrie aad eiget others, charged with rioting and with the murder of James Curran, came on. The charges arose out of the riots at Queen's Island Shipyard. Belfast, on the 4th June. The grand jury ignored the bill against Norman Finite and the other cases were adjourned till next assizes, on the ground that the Crown witnesses were afraid to give evidence in consequence of the relgious feeling which prevailed at Belfast. Tern S runm.—Two MEN DRowerEn. Manchester and other parts of Lancashire, and the North of England gener- ally, were visited 09 Wednesday by a severe thunderstorm, accompanied by a heavy downpour of rain. In connection with the storm a sad accident is reported from Liverpool. Five men were in a sewer at Toxteth Park, doing some re- pairs, when the storm burst, and the water rushed through the sewer with such for ce that two of them were washed awey and drowned. The Other three escaped with @Vas catty. . A WAR VESSEL IN COLLISION.—On Tuesday morning a serious collision occurred off Portland between H.M.S. Northimpton and a four-mated iron ship—Crofton Hall, of Liverpool—in ballast. The Northampton, in company with several other ironclads, was coming up the Channel for Spithead, when she ran into the Crofton Hall, smash- iag ber bows and inflicting considerable damage. Fortu- Inately the injury was lust above water line, and with assistance the Craton Hall was brought int) Portland Harbour. , LAWLESSNESS ter IRELAND.—A force of police has been despatched from Oban to Tiree to put down the lawlessness of the Land League on that island. The large farm of Greenhill was relinquished by the tenant on Whitsunday, and it was subsequently re-taken by a Mr. M‘Neil. who was a member of the Land League. His fellow-Leaguers, how- ever, refused to let him take possession, drove off his cattle, and put on their own, levying fines also on the transgressing crofters. The police have orders to put down this lawless- combination. DISASTROUS MILL Frites AT HEYWCOD.—Between twelve o'clock and half-pest on Tuesday morning a fire, supposed to be caused by spontaneous combustion, Was discovered to have broken out at Mr. Edward Tatrereall's, Bridge Mill, Park-street, Hopwood, Heywood. The building was com- pletely .gutted. and the damage will amount to at least £20,000. It is partially covered by ißsurance in the Mutual, Norwich Union, and Commercial Union offices. The dames illuminated the distrust for miles around, and I attracted thousands of persons to the spot. A VESSEL BLOWN UP BY DYNAMITE .—The Italian cut- ter San Carol, from Genoa, with about three tons of dyna- mite on Board, has been blown up by an explosion when about eight miles off the island of Monte Christo and 30 from Elba. The captain and crew, noticing a little smoke issuing from a crack, at once took to the boats, and thus saved their lives. They bad rowed about a mile from the vessel when it blew up, with a report that was heard at Elba. Pieces of the wreck fell in the boat. A botanist tethering herbs at Monte Christo was thrown to the ground. by the shock. Sszeons FIRE IN BOOTLE.—On Monday morning a fire broke out in a seven-storey warehouse in Baltic-street and Strand-street, Bootle. The four lower storeys were filled with cotton. and in the storey above there was a large quantity of beans stored. It was soon seen that the contents and in- terior of the building could not be saved. At about a quar- ter past two o'clock the flaor of the building fell in, and by three o'clock the fire was practically got under. The damage to the cotton and beans is estimated at £20,000, and that to the warehouse about £6,000. The buLding and contents were both insured. WAYLAYING PROTESTANTS IN IRELAND.—At London- derry Asiezes on Monday, before Justice Lawson, Michael M•Cenn, Thomas Logan. Thomas NleNally, Michael Fergus' son, Francis Hampsey, Daniel M‘Nally, and Thomas INl`Cann were indicted for waylaying Protestants returning from Cookstown on May 15. All were found guilty, but Fergus- son was recommended to mercy. Thomas M'Cann, liamp- s:y, and Thomas M‘Nally were sentenced to twelve months' imprisonment each. Fereueson was discharged, and the remainder were sentenced to six months each. The jury acquitted five Protestants charged in a cross case. ONLY A MISTAKE. A humourons error recently took place in a love affair in Kentucky. A crimple of young folks agreed to elope together, and by some mistake in the preliminary arrangements the male lover put his ladder up to the window next to that where his sweetheart slept, which proved to be that where her mamma, a handsome widow, reposed. She turned the mistake to her advantage. got into his arms, returned hie embraces, was borne by him to the carriage, and by preserving a becoming silence until daylight, kept him in error, and then, by the potent power of her blandishments, actually charmed him into matrix:teeny with herself. TERRIBLE AFFRAY BETWEEN BROTRERS.—Late on Satur- day night a stabblnE affray between brothers, which threatens a fatal termination, took place at Penycae, near r guaboraDenbigleshire. Under the intliterce of liquor, two r brothers, George and William Jackson, bask t makers,quar- relied and fought, and George. while his brother was upon the ground, drew his pocket knife and stabbed him with it several times, inflicting serious wounds, from which he bled copiously. The kisife was wrested from George Jackson by bystanders, and he immediately ran home and returned with another knife, when he was taken into cueody. But faint hopes are entertained of the recovery of the wounded mall. REMAPKABLE IRISR MURDER Turah.—At Cork Assizes. in Menday, e mysterious murder trial commenced, the pri- soner beine John O'Neill, who is charged with shooting llaniel O'Neill, near Clonykilty, in April last. The poor old man was sitting in his cabin with Its wife at night, when a arrange man entered and fired a revolver at him and then disappeared. The shot was a fatal one, and O'Neill fell lead. Subsequently the prisoner was arrested in the Cavan Workhouse, and, strange to relate, was recognised as the son of the murdered man, who was thought to be in America. This he woutly denied, notwithstaading that persons who hid known him before he emigrated to Amerce many years ten swore to his identity. His arrest at the Workhouse three weeks after the murder was followed by the finding of a revolver which was concealed wader a hedge, not far from he Workhouse. The Crown allege that this weapon be- longed to the accused, and that it was with this he mur- tered his father. The case from is einning to end is of a nog extraordinary nature, the ceetemsranees that the ac- eised denies all knowledge of tbe crime and repudiates any etationship with the murdered man creating great interest in the trial.

div.p: By Mr. THOMAS WHITEHEAD.
By .21Ir: J. H. TOW...I7LEY.

MR. GLADSTONE, as was anticipated, has accepted the verdict of the country as against him, and has tendered his resignation. He has not even waited for Parliament to be called together next month ; he regards it as in the interest of the State that the present crisis should be brought to an end as speedily as possible ; and that his opponents, if they have a policy, should, as soon as possible, bring their policy into operation. Unfortu- nately for the Tories, but fortunately for the country, Lord SALISBURY is not in a position to command a majority, and the incoming Government will have to do as it can, and not as it will. If Lord HARTINGTON • would only at the last moment listen to the pathetiC cry—" Come over and help us !" the Con- servatives would be made happy. They do not want Mr. CHAMBERLAIN; but they would like to absorb Lord HARTINGTON; he would be a good exchange, they think, for Lord DERBY, whose removal from their ranks left a gap which has never been filled. But Lord HARTINGTON is not by any means inclined to be swallowed up; he is a Liberal who looks forward to a future in which he will be again acting with the Liberal party; and, wiser thin ESAU, he declines to barter away his birthright for a mess of pottage. He has often stood aloof from Mr. GLADSTONE, and he is likely to stand aloof from Lord SAMS' BURY. It must be galling to the Conserva- tives to feel that he is arbiter of their fate. But there is no help for it; they must learn to play a straight game, if they would have a straight win. Last year they relied upon the Parnellites to give them a majority at the polls; but they didn't succeed in getting what they wanted. This year they have traded on the division in the ranks of the Liberal party; and yet they are not happy—they have not obtained a working majority. Lord SALISBURY will form a Government; but it will be a Government on sufferance. The Cabinet will be unable to do anything without taking counsel, sweet or otherwise) with the authority outside the Cabinet. Lord HARTINGTON will be the Con- sulting Politician of the Conservative party.; with power to say —"You must take my act-i vice or your Administration will go to the wall.' But let us look ahead; let it be supposed that the Tory Government is formed, and that an attempt is being made to carry out the policy of the 26th january—the policy 0S "the suppression of the 'National League. Is it not obvious that not a step could be taken unless it was known that the member for Rossendale and his Unionist followers approved of that course? But are theY likely to accept any such proposal? We think not. The CHAMBERLAIN section would revolt against coercion as " a hatefui

incident;" and there are few, indeed, of Lord HARTINGTON'S immediate supporters who would hear of such a thing. It is not too ; much to say that, although the Tories would . doubtless dearly like to punish the Parnel- lites by putting the bulk of them in gaol under a new Coercion Act, they will not have the opportunity of gratifying their feelings in that particular way ; it will not he to the taste of the Consulting Politician. 1. Lord SAILsBuRy, foreseeing this, may set about preparing some scheme of local self- ' government for Ireland, not with a view to ' /fleeting the views of such politicians as Ford CARNARVON, who have some regard for - Irish aspirations. but with the object of satis- fying the Liberal Unionists. There is a bare Possibility—not a probability—that he might Bucceed in this, for since Lord HARTING:I:ON has shown sign of moving in this direction there is hope that his pace might be so acce- -lerated as to bring him pretty well on to the Position now occupied by Mr. -CHAMBER- • • I-Ars. The "views of the Tories themselves need not be taken into account. A Prime kinister who has had a Home Ruler :as his Irish Lord Lieutenant will not stick at any- thing that stops short of Home Rule, if it Will keep him office for a year or two. It roust also be borne in mind that there may be some amongst the followers of Mr. GLADs-roNE who would support any bill that gave the Irish greater control over their own affairs than they at Dtesent exercise ; they would take a Slice of the loaf as being better than no bread., A Tory self-government bill for Ireland once through the House of Commons. Would, however imperfect, be in friendly Ihands when it reached the House of Lords; and in this way it might, in a comparatively short time, get upon the statute boor:, Not that that would settle the matter ; the question will never be settled by any Measure which falls short of giving the People of Ireland a Parliament of their own. But assuming a Tory Government passed some kind of bill for the government of Ire- land—and that is assuming a great deal— bow long woul(d, they be likely tosurvive with the Libo.ials and Dissentienttiberals opposed to them on the very next issue that might arise? The Irish question disposed of, the life of a Tory Administration would not be Worth a month's purchase. The Tories know this ; and it is not, therefore, likely that they would seek death by resorting to legislation. The policy which would be most to their humour would be one of "masterly inactivity" ; and it is one which would or a while at any rate—be best for the country. The various sections of the Liberal party re- quire time to come together and adjust their differences. There has already been too much of bitterness imported into, the family quarrel; and it would be well if Liberals and Liberal Unionists would now direct their at- tention to the movements of the Tories to ensure that when they came into office they Shall be powerless for mischief. "Sweet are the uses of adversity " ; we welcome the re- Signation of Mr. GLADSTONE as a means of throwing the burden of responsibility upon the Tories, and as the first step towards re- uniting the Liberal party.

SEVERAL publicans and beer-sellers were brought before the St. Helens migistrates on Monday, arid fined £5 and costs for breach of the Lotteries and Betting Acts. So long as there is a law against these offences, it ought to be enforced rigidly and systemati- cally. The magistrates were disposed to be lenient, because. as the CHAIRMAN alleged, there had been no cases since i 884.. With regard to this. uperintendent JOHNSON said It was not that betting had not been carried cm, but becFuse it was difficult to obtain Eufficient evidence to convict offenders. In the cases in question. the police authorities had found it necessary to send out, along with an informer who acted as a decoy duck, two policemen who were attired as working- men. There is something repulsive in this mode of procedure; but what are the police to do ? It is their business, it is true, not to create offences, but to bring offenders to justice ; but, on the other hand, if they have good reason to know the law is being broken, they are justified in testing the matter for themselves. It can- not be pleasant fora publican to know that his house is being watched on account or Sunday drinking ; but it does not much mat- ter, after all, to the landlord who does not supply liquor within the prohibited hours. And so with betting houses; if those who are suspected of keeping them open will take care not to make bets of any kind, they will soon cease to be troubled with policemen dressed as working-men. Offenders against the Lotteries Act are in an exceptional posi- tion; they are sinners in so far as they break the law, but it is impossible not to feel a little sympathy for them, seeing that the law is not administered impartially. If ELIZA- BETH LITTLER, of the Young Prince beerhouse, is to be " fined f 5 and i4.s costs" for selling tickets in "The Welbeck Cup Lottery," we do not see why Lady Bountiful should not be fined for keeping open a lottery at a Church or Chapel Bazaar. It is the duty of magis- trates to administer the law, not to draw distinctions in applying it ; and so long as lotteries are illegal they should be put down all round. Justice ceases to be justice when it becomes obvious that there is one law for the rich and another for the poor. We know that a good deal can be said in favour of permitting lotteries for charitable objects; and we know, too, that much more can be said against it. But that is not the point in these particular cases. As the law stands, it applies to lotteries generally, and it is a public scandal to bring it into operation against publicans, while sinners in silks are left untouched. Let justice be done though the heavens fall, but let it be justice.

----- THE WIDNES CODN'TY CRICKETER.—The career of Mr. J. Briggs, the Lancashire county. cricketer, is watched with the greatest interest in Widnes and neighbourhood. His father is at present professional to the club of the chemical centre, for many years young Jack lived in the town and took part in all athletic exercises, and he is lo international upon to some extent as a native. H i is success n the match, "England v. Australia," this week, when England defeated the Colonials by an in.mings and 10G runs, has been hailed with enthusiasm by all who take an interest in the game, and who know the modest young cricketer. Describing the finish of the match, the "Sporting Chronicle" said :—" This result is not a little owing to the capital bowling of little Briggs. who supplemented his excellent per- formance in the first innings by taking six wickets for 45 runs—a magnificent feat against such bats- men. During the match he has taken 11 for 74 This is the more satisfactory, as plenty of critics found fault with his . selection, but Briggs has amply proved that he .is worth his place in any eleven. At the conclusion of the match there was a scene of tremendous enthusiasm. Several hundreds of the spectators assembled in front of the pavilion and indulged in rounds of cheering. Briggs came in for a great reception, being carried shoulder high to the telegraph office by the excited crowd, whose attentions must have been rather embarrassing. .Barlow was also warmly cheered."

TEACHERS PICNIC AT RUNCORN.—Tne annual picnic of the teachers of the Camden Wesleyan Sunday School took place on Monday, when they went by train to Betws-y- Coed, and spent a delightful day. DESERTION OF FAMILY AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Police Court on Wednesday, Joseph Lowe, a chemical Labourer, was charged with deserting his wife and family, and leaving them chargeable to the common fund of the Union. Mr. Ward. relieving officer, proved the case, and the prisoner was sentenced to fourteen days' hard labour. Fecievert SERVICE AT RUNCoRN.—A flower service was held on Sunday at Camden Wesleyan School. The room was adorned with plaets from the conservatories of Mrs. Heel e- burst, The Grange, and the children brought boquets of flowers. The Rev. George Woods delivered an appropriate address. The flowers were on Monday sent to the Widnes Accident Hospital. FLOWER SERVICE AT WIDNES.—On Sunday a flower ser- vice was held in Slitter.? Congregational Chapel, Widnes. The edifice Was appropriately adorned with flowers, and the members of the congregation also brought offerings. The Rev. R. G. Hughes, the pastor, occupied the pulpit both morning and evening,, and the congregations were of fair proportions. The choir rendered specially selected music, and collections were made on behalf of the chapel funds. RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.—Tnescliy, before His Honour Judge Wynne Ffonlkes. The list comprised 6 judgment summomer, 1 adjourned plaint, and 139 original plaints. The only case of interest was one in which Thomas Dutton, junior, of Weston Point, sued Charles Johnson, of Maple- street, Manchester, beerhonse keeper, for £24 10-3 61, money lent to the defendant's wife and interest. Mr. Burton ap- peared for the plaintiff. At ter the evidence had been given His Horeour held that the wite had ne authority to Pledge her husband's credit, and gave a verdict for the de- fendant. ACCIDENT ON RUNCORN BRIDGE.—Shortly before twelve o'clock on Monday night, an old man named William Ab- bott was picked up on the approach to Runcorn Bridge, at the Cheshire side, bleeding from a wound in the head. It was at first thought that he had been attacked while cross- ing the bridge, but an 'inquiry revealed the fact that when coining down the inclined footpath on the Cheshire side he fell with his head against the ticket office. The injured man, who suffered from loss of blood, was conveled to the surgery of Dr. Mangan. where his wound was dressed. As he had no residence in Runcorn; he was allowed to remain at the police station until Tuesday morning. DROWNED AT WESTON POINT.-0.1 Monday Mr. T. E. SiTorsley, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Weaver Hotel, Weston Point, on the body of D mid Dunnett, a sailor, of Dunnett, Caithness. On Friday afternoon the do• ceased and another sailor named James Calder were paint- ing the chic of the vessel " Queen of the Isles," and for that purpose were standing on a ladder which was slung by ropes. The ladder broke and beth men fell into the water. Calder succeeded in keeping himself afloat until rescued, but Dunnett disappeared beneath the surface, and his body was not recovered for a quarter of an hour, when life was qaite extinct. A verdict of Accidental death " was re- corded. FLOWER SERVICES AT RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH. On Monday afternoon a children's flower service was held at Runcorn Parish Church. The children brought offerings of flowers which were used to decorate the edifies. 'The Rev. T. M. Arrnson preached the sermon. In the evening another flower service was held, a larger congreption as, emblin. and the floral offerings were numerous and beau- tiful, The Rev. E. D. "TOUCH AND GO." Sir Clamles Dilke has made bad worse by asking for the intervention of the Queen's Proctor. He has staked everything upon the re4nit of the trial—and lost. The Queen has accepted the resignation of Kr. Gladstone and has sent for Lord Salisbury. It was suggested the other day that the Duke of Argyll should be made Prime Minister ; but why did people smile when they heard of it and say—' God bless the Duke of Argyll?" Mr. Goschen's chance has come at last. If he will only promise to be a good boy and not run riot, the Tories will be disposed to find him two seats ; one in Parliament and another in the Cabinet. He has too long tried to sit on two stools—a Liberal stool and a Tory stool—and has come to the ground. There let him lie, or let the Tories pick him up.

A London correspondent says :—" Tt is as- sumed by the younger men that Sir Richard Cross is to be got rid of." This is appalling. Can it mean that the dynamitards are on his track ? Or does it refer to the possibility of the member for the Newton Division being shunted when the Tory Cabinet is formed ? It would never do to leave him out in the cold; there would be no one to "reply to Air. Gladstone."

The prospectus of the Manchester Ship Canal Company was issued on Tuesday, and it is stated that a large number of shares have been taken up, though the response has not been equal to expectations. There has been nothing paid for promotion money, the Provisional Committee having given their services. The Stock Exchange, in- fluenced by the large railway interest, has not a good word to say, but that is a matter cf course under the circumstances.
