SA.LE OF' WORI AT HOUGH GREEN.—For the purpose of making up the deficiency of £3O in the organ and heating fund in connection with St. Michael's Parish Church, Hough Green, a sale of work, consisting of useful and fa.ncy needlework, was opened in the Church school-room, on Thursday afternoon. The articles for sale were principally what had been left over from the bazaar held last year, but in addition to these there were also on sale goods which bad been made purposely for the present occasion. There were five stalls alitogether. Three of them, at which general articles for wear and ornament were dispensed, were pre- sided over by the following ladies :—Mrs. C. W. Wooll, Miss Smith, Mrs. Gerard. Miss Bratley, Miss A. Turton, Miss Thompson, Miss Booth, and Miss M. Booth. At the flower stall, on which were some beautiful plants, bouquets, and buttonholes, the wants of customers were attended to by the Misses Hodgkinson and Lucas, while Mrs. R. Lewis, Miss Payne, Miss Garnett, and Miss Moss presided at the refresh- ' ment stall. During the afternoon there were not many per- sons present, and business did not proceed as briskly as ! might have been desired, but no doubt the small attend- ance was owing to the unpropitious state of the weather. In the evening, however, when the Widnes Church of England Temperance Society's brass band discoursed a variety of music, and entertainments of various character took place, the attendance was much larger. Maur OF BOWLS AT RIINCORN.—An important and in- teresting main of bowls, 21 up, was held at the green of the South Bank Hotel, Runcorn, on Tuesday and Wednesday. There were 64 entries, and the proprietor (Mr. Thos. Jones) added £5 to the entrance fees to be divided into prizes. There were therefore some valuable prizes to be competed for, and the best bowlers is the surrounAing district were attracted to the main. The green was in capital order, and the arrangements carried out under the superintendence of the proprietor and Mr. Robert Wright were admirable. On the first slay the weather was beautifully fine, but shortly after noon on Wednesday a storm broke over the town and put an end to the play for several hours. In consequence the final was not played off until nearly eleven o'clock at! night, and .despite the difficulties under which they la- boured, both Mr_ (3 leave and Mr. Birch played remarkably well, and an exciting finish resulted. The game was 20 all, when Mr. Birch run the block and knocked himself out. Rl:remora/ FnEs Puntac LIBRARY' COMMITTEE.—The monthly meeting was held on Monday evening. Mr.F.A.Lake presided, and there were present Messrs. Moss, Norman, and Jones (librarian). The Librarian reported that during the past month there had been 674 books issued, lejne a de- crease on the corresponding period of last year, The sum of 17s lid bad been received for fines, 2s 4d for catelogues, 12s for tickets, and 6s 7d for sale of papers. The Librarian also presented his annual report, which stated that the cem- reittee recorded with pleasure that the efforts made during the year to provide reading for the public had been greatly appreciated. The library had been open on 150 days, and the number of issues had been 18,266, being an increase of 2,648 over the previous year. The daily averare ot issues was 121. During the year 718 borrowers' tickets had been issued, hsing an increase of 110 over the previous year. During the year 461 volumes had been added to the library, 314 of which had been purchased and 147 pre- Rented. The total number of volumes at present in the library was 3,577, of which 785 were works of reference. The reading-room had been inconveniently crowded durinu the year. and the committee had made a request for addi- tional accommodation, and hoped that by next winter the difficulty would be overcome, and an opportunity afforded for a more quiet study of the works in Vae reference depart- ment. The committee tendered their thanks to the donors of money, books, papers, and periodicals, without whose aid the carrying on of tbn library would be rendered extremely I difficult. The report was ordered to be printed. There was no other business of public interest.

Mr. Gladstone regards kindness as "ever nobler than revenge." He has nominated to the vacant office of Deputy Chairman of the Board of Inland Revenue, Viscount St. Cyres, the son of Lord Iddesleigh. He does not object to give a good berth to a Tory provi- ding the Tory is a good man. It is very gratifying to learn that Mr. Mun- della has appointed Mr. John Burnett, secre- tary to the Amalgamated Society of En- gineers, to the office of labour correspondent in the new Labour Bureau. Mr. Bradlaugh is entitled to some credit for having called the aitention of Parliament to the necessity of moving in this direction. -- British consuls in foreign countries will doubtless be called upon to furnish informa- tion to the Labour Bureau ; but they might with advantage go a little furthei, and keep the Government at home well post-d in everything of moment that relates to trade and commerce. Continental Governments make good use of their agents in " pushing business," and if we would keep Dace we must do the same. A fair field and no favour —that is all we need ask. Since receiving the letter from Mr. John Ashley, which will be found in our correspon- dence columns, we have caused special in- quiries to be made, and find that the state- ments of Costello and Mannion as to the drinking at Wilderspool Brewery, on the day after the election, are without the slightest foundation. It would now seem, on further inquiry, that the two men must have inven- ted the extraordinary story when brought before the magistrates. We, of course, withdraw every observation we had made on the case, and deeply regret commenting on statements reflecting on Sir Gilbert Greenall, M.P., and the firm with which he is con- nected—statements which we have ourselves proved to be without found3.tion.

BOWERS PATENT SEPARATOR.—ThiS invention is ir.ended to effect a separation of the mineral salts and other impurities which exist in the feed i water used for steam boilers. This process s of great advantage to steam users, in not only pre- venting the formation of scale and deposit in their boilers, but, as the process is automatic, frequent stoppages for cleansing are not required, and boilers fitted with the apparatus can be worked for long periods without being opened. To accomplish this object advantage is taken of the natural laws of gravity, producing motion in an ascending and de- scending column of water of different tempera- tures. The separator has been working at -Messrs. Wood and Wright's, Clayton, and also at the Bruns- wick Mills, Bradford-road, Ancoats, Manchester, with marked success. No less than 2cwt. of solid matter has been taken out of .a boiler in one month by means of the apparatus, without the aid of com- positions. The boiler, on being examined, was found to be free from all loose slutch, and the two or three plates which had been thoroughly cleansed were in six months time quite free from scale. Messrs. Geo. W. Allen and Co., 63, York-chambers, Braze- nose-street, Manchester, are the introducers of this
patent.

LOCAL VOLUNTEERS AT WIMBLEDON.—The 18 representatives of the 21st L.R.V. (St. Helens) who journeyed to Wimbledon to take part in the annual shooting competitions have rendered a good. account and return with prizes and prize money 'to a large amount. In the competition for the Queen's Prize, Sergeant W. Dwerryhouse, with a total score of 239 points, won £8 and a badge, Corporal G. Taylor, 235, secured..Es, and Private R. McGill, 170, won £4. In the StoGeorgel contest; Private R. Norbury, with a score of 33, won a prize of £lO, with a jewel and badge; while Ser- geant F. J. West won £4, and Sergeant Dwerry- house £2, in the Alexandra competition. In the Alfred contest Sergeant C. C. Wilson won £5, Ser- geant West £3, and Sergeant W. Junor £3. ser- gean'3 West further won £2 in the Windmill com- petition, ..E2 in the "Daily Telegraph" contest, and a similar amount in the Martin's Cup. In the latter event Private R. Norbury also won .C 2 and Sergeant Wil- son also won OE2 in the "Daily Telegraph" contest. Sergeant West appeared to great advantage in the "All-corners Aggregates," for which he won £2O, and Sergeant Wilson won £2, and in the "Grand" contest Sergeant Wilson won a bronze cross and .E 5. In the "English Twenty," Sergeant West won £l, and Corporal G. Taylor £5. In the international competition for the Kolapore Cup, Sergeant West had the honour of winning £3, while in the United Service Challenge Cup contest Sergeant West was selected as one of the eight to represent the volun- teers against the other branches of the service. He was fourth on the results,- and won £5. Altogether the representatives of the 21st L.R.V. have won _ during the competition. £lOl 8s in prize money, six badges, one jewel, and one bronze cross. 60nt BTRTHDAY OF LORD DERBY.--10n Wednes- day Lord Diirby celebrated his 60th birthday. His lordship, who is the eldest son of the fourteenth Earl of Derby, was born at Knowsley on the 21st of July, 1826, was educated at Rugby, and at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he took a first-class in classics in 1848. His lordship, ;who was an unsuc- cessful candidate for Lancaster, in March 1848, was, during his absence in America, elected Lord G. Bentinck's successor. for Lynn Regis, which he continued to represent as Lord Stanley until he suc- ceeded to the peerage. He was appointed Under- Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs in, March, 1852, in Lord Derby's first Administration. He be- came Secretary of State for India with a 'seat in the Cabinet under Lord Derby's second Administration in 1858-9. Hinordship was appointed 'Secretary of IState for Foreign Affairs in Lord Derby's third Ad- ministration in July, 1866. He held the seals of the Foreign Office until the accession of Mr. Glad- stone to power in December, 1868. His 'lordship was installed Lord Rector of the University of Glas- gow on the Ist April, 1869. In 1874, NO= Mr. Dis- raeli formed his Cabinet, Lord Derby was again en- 'trusted with the seals of the Foreign Office. In 1878 he left the Conservative Government, and at the latter end of 1879 detached himself definitely from the Conservative organisations. . He was sworn in as Secretary of State for the Colonies in Mr. Gladstone's Administration in December, 1882. In 1874 he was eleated Rector of the University of Edinburgh. Before his success to the peerage, his lordship served as a member of the Royal Commis- sion on Army Purchase in 1856-7; on the Univer- tity Commission in 1856-60; and on the Commission on the organisation of the Indian Army in 1858-9. He was chairman of the Commission on the Sanitary State of the Indian Army in 1859-61, and was on the Commission on Patents in 18634. His lordship we are glad to state, enjoys excellent health.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting of this board was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. The chair WAS occupied by Lieut.- Col. Ashton, and there were also present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood, cud Messrs. Hadfield, Aaron, High- field, Hall, Mclntyre, Whitlow, 11. Linaaer (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk) —Dr. J. Adams, medical edicer for the authority's district, submitted the following quarterly report :—I have to report that during the quarter ending 'Jun, 30th, 18S6, the registrar's returns record 151 births and 72 deaths, in the four registration sub-districts comprised in the rural sanitary district of the Runcorn Union. Of the births 81 were males and 70 females ; birth rate 7.5 per 1,000 per quarter (or 300 per 1 000 per annum). against 149 births, with a birth rate of 7 4 per 1,000 per quarter (or 296 per 1,000 per annum), in the corresponding quarter of 1885. Of the deaihs 31 were males and 41 fe- males; death rate 3.6 per 1,000 per quitter (or 14 4 per 1,000 per annum) against 101 deaths, with a death rate of 5 0 per 1,000 per quarter (or 20 0 per 1,000 per annum) in the corresponding quarter of 18'2.5. Of the deaths 14 oc- curred in persens under 1 year of age, 7 occurred in per- sons between the ages of 1 and 5 years. 33 oc- curred in persons between the ages of 5 and 60 years, 18 in persons of 60 years and upwards. The causes of death are set forth in the an- nexed tabular statement. It is gratifying for me to be able to state that this is the lowest death rate I have yet recorded in a quarterly report. There has been an entire absence of deaths from serieus zy mode affections, while ten of the 72 deaths are c,lairned by phthisis alone. There have been only two cases referred to the coroner."— The report was considered satiefactory.—The Clerk stated that the committee appointed to inset a committee cf the Highway Board of Daresbury respecting the stopping by the Authority of road drain inlets to sewer and orain, met at Steckton Heath on the 12th inst. After inspecting the line of sewer and the position of the several grids and con- nections which had been stopped, and the clerk haviog read the complaint of the Highway B card and the explana- tion of the inspector, and, it also appearing from a fur- ther statement made by the surveyor that the road drain was cut across by the sewer and never made good, and that the mere restoration of the grids and catclipits would not remedy the evil complained of, it was resolved that the Sanitary Authority be recommended to have the road drain, where crossed by the sewer, examined and made good where necessary, and that the grids and connections, with the road drain, be restored and made good at the expense of the Authority, so that the water from the highway can flow into the usual channel, into which it ran before the Author- ity interfered with it.—The report was adopted on the pro- position of Mr. Mclntyre, seconded by Mr. Aaron.—On the proposition of Mr, Hadfield, seconded. by Mr. Aaron, it was decided that Mr. Farrington, sanitary inspector, should keep a diary of the work done by him, to he submitted to the Authority at their fortnightly meetings.—Tuis was the business.

div.head: ALLEGED OUTRAGE BY IRISHMEN AT RUNCORN. THREE MEN SERIOUSLY INJURED.
div.p: ALLEGED OUTRAGE BY IRISHMEN AT RUNCORN. THREE MEN SERIOUSLY INJURED.

An outrage at present surrounded by considerable ?nystery took place at the village of Halton. So far as can be gleaned, it appears that three men named Richard Moores, John Powell, and Henry Barker, were in Runcorn on Satur- day evening, and returned to Helton shortly before mid- Moores parted with his companions at Halton Brook, and B erker and Powell remained together having a "chat." When "Good night" had been exchanged, BAI ker was set upon by six Irish harvestmen. He was knocked down, kicked, and stabbed in the thigh. Powell, who went to his assistance, was also brutally maltreated, and then the men decamped. Shortly afterwards Moores was found lying unconscious in a pool of his own blood at the bottom of Halton Fields. He was bleeding from numerous wounds in the bead, and was badly bruised in various parts of the body. He had to be carried home. His assailants had evidently left him for deal. Information was given to the Police, and next day Sergeants Neild and Lowndee, and Constables Sutton and Jackson, searched the farms in the neighbourhood. At Yew Tree Farm they found two hats and a belt belonging to the injured men, and succeeded in. arresting six Irishmen, five of whom gave the name of Farrell, and the sixth that of Lawrence Giblin. One of the Farrells had his hand bandaged. and it was found that he had been stabbed, the wound penetrating right through the hand. The men admitted that they had been engaged. in a quarrel the previous night, but alleged that they were at- tacked first, and only acted in self-defence. At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. C. Reynolds and Mr. A. Thomas, Lawrence Giblin, Michael Ferrell, James Farrell, James Farrell, Henry Farrell, Thos. Farrell, and Denis Farrell, were charged with feloniously doing grievous bodily harm to Richard Moores, John Powell, and Henry Barker. Superintendent Hollingsworth said he should call medical testimony, and ask for the men to be remanded, as he was not prepared to go on with the cuss. Dr. Carruthers said that at one o'clock on Sunday morn- ing he was called ti see Richard Moores. He found him suffering frrm eight incised wounds on the forehead and head, and several bruise, about the body. He also saw Barker, who was suff ring from a punctured wound in the thigh. Mores would not be able to attend for a week, and Barker could not walk at present. The prisoners were remanded until Friday. „ The prisoners were conveaed to Knutsford gaol by the afternoen train, and their departure was witnessed by a large crowd. There were many sympathisers with the pri- soners pr sent, and they frequently shouted to the men to keep their hearts up. Much diseppeintment was caused by the railway officials refusing to allow the people on the platform, and angry cries were raised. " Home Rule for ever" was shouted by same person in the crowd, and then there were opposing cries given utterance to. A disturbance WAR the result. Several women engaged in a fight with two men, and getting the worst of it pulled off their clogs, which they used with startling effect. Two men bled copiously from wounds in the head, and others bore signs of the women's prowess. The women followed the men along Lowlands-Told, and indulg-d in stone throwing. One man, who went in a boat for the purpose of washing his wounds. fell into the water, but he was rescued. The dist:it-trine, was quickly quelled ma the arrival of the police.—The prisoners were again brought before the magistrates yester- day. Suppriamdent Hollingsworth said Muores war still unable to attend, and he asked for, and was granted a remand until this morning.
BBITISII AND FOREIGN BIBLE SOCIETY. ANNUAL MEETIIIG OF THE WIDNES BRANCH.

The annual meeting of the Widnes Branch of the British and Foreign Bible Society was held on Tuesday evening in Lacey- street School-room, Widnes. Toe Rev. J. Wright-Williams (vicar of Widnes) presided, and there were also present the Revs. R. Burden and J, HothersaT I, and Mr. Jelinger Symons. deputation. There was only a small attendance. The meet- ing opened with devotional exercises, the Chairman after- wards cal lieg upon the secretary of the local branch of the society (the Rev. R. Burden) to read his report. —The Sec- retary said after balancing up last year there was a small amount in hand of Li 8s 11d. The collection at the last annual meeting was £1 53 41. The offertories at St. Paul's Church amounted to £3 103, and he was thankful to say that Mr. Williams had brought another amount like that that evening. Mr. Williams had been kind enough to have an offertory at his church on behalf of tie society, and he ' had a very great sense of obligation to him for so doing. The sales had been .E 2 16s Bd, and there had been colleeed by Miss Hudson £3 63 Gd, and by Mrs Robinson £1 us 6d, making a total altogether of receipts of £l3 183 11d. The expereli- tore had been as follows :—Scripturee Ll 8/, 48 new testa- ments 4s, Bibles 16s 61, commission 7s id, carriage and postage le, printing 16e 6d, donation to parent society £9 93, and Messrs. Mackie and Co. 3s 61, leaving a balance in hand of 133 4d.—Mr. Jelinger E. Symons, tv ho was received ; with applause, then delivered an interesting address, in the course of which he alluded to the large number of deaths , Which had occurred during the past year on the staff of the British and Foreign Bible Society', mentioning specially thst of the president, Lord Shaftesbury, Lord Cairns, one of the vice-presidents, and Bishop Frazer, of Manchester, who had rendered the so- ciwy very efficient support. They had also to larrlnt the death of the Dean of Chester and others, including Mr. Orme, their late treasurer. During the past year over four million copies of the scriptures had been circulate .1 by their 1: society, and when they considered that there were nume- rous other societies engaged in the same work :is themselves be thouAt that was something to be proud of. (Hear, hear.) The speaker then dilated on the work done by the society in various ports of the world, and said though some- times the colnorteurs, or the society's agents, met wall re- buffs, they were generally well received. At the conclusion of the address votes of thanks were accorded Mr. Symons, end the chairman, and these two gentlemen having replied, the Benediction was pronounced and the meeting ter- minated
NEW SALVATION ARIII- BA.RRACKS AT RUNCORN.

Last evening a new Salvation Army barracks was opened 1 at Runcorn. For several years past the branch of the army stationed at Runcorn. have used the Foresters' 11411, in Devonshire-squere, and occasionally, the Public Hall for their services. This means of accommodation Leing con- sidered unsuitable the plot of land on which the old hell ' stood was secured on lease, and there now occupies the site of the ancient structure, a plain brick building capable of accommodating 1,200 persons. In its construction the stones of the oil hall have been utilised, and the building is of a very substantial character. The interior is also very plain, but well adapted for its in- tended purpose. There is a capital platform, arranged in tiers, which will bold unwards of a hundred persons and at the rear of. the room there is a galhry. Mr. Cox- head, contractor, London, has carried our— the entire work, at a cost of about £1,500. Adjoining ths barracks are the captain's quarters, what was originally a stable, having been transformed into a sui,abie residence for the leader of the local corps, Ceptein Moor. General Booth, who was to take the chief part in the proceedings, arrieed in town shortly before six, anti was met at the station by a large number of his followers. Subsequently there was a " royal proces- sion" heeded by a" war charite," drawn by a couple of grey harass, and in which was seated the general. Following was a brass band and a " host of warriors," including many officers and members of the army frem the surrounding towns, bearing bennerettes of various hue and device. At I the meeting which was subsequently held in the " Bar-1 racks." a vigorous address was given by General. Booth. Cornmissiener Sherwood also gave some particulars as to the cost of the bnilding, and said a debt of £250 rested upon it. Mr. George Marshall, the treasurer, I had given two sums of £25, arid Mr. Richardson, the !Secretary and his wife had each given £lO. Mr. Marshall I likewise made a short address. A collection was made, and I the usual "canaries " for pro:nises to give money towards ;the reduction of the debt.

Lord Hartington, Mr. Bright, nor Mr. Chamberlain finds a corner seat vacant on any given night. The interest in the Crawford case culminated on Tuesday and yesterday, when Mrs. Crawford was in the box. But it has been maintained throughout at a very high level. Never perhaps was such a piti- ful story unfolded in a public court. The people least moved by it seem those• who have taken a I prominent part in the domestic drama. It was, in advance, rather embarrassing that Sir Charles Dilke and Mr. Crawford should meet day by day, almost rubbing shoulders on a bench, in full view of the public. Yet none of the parties concerned appear to feel awkward. Mrs. Crawford is supported by the company of her two sisters, Mrs. Ashton Dilke and Mrs. Harrison, and to see them laughing and chat- ting, very much as if they were in a theatre, is amazing. Sir Charles Dilke sits next but one to Mr. Crawford. A shorthand writer separates Mr. Crawford from the three fair sisters; but that is all. Sir Charles Dilke was evidently in a state of great nervousness whilst in the box. This he bravely attempted to hide by assuming an air of indifference and a readiness to discuss the matter which was a little repellant. Having nothing to hide, he was al- ways attempting to make little speeches, a tendency which the judge, once at least, checked with some sternness. Mrs. Crawford telling her shameful story was as self-possessed and innocent looking as she probably was when in the afternoon she joined her husband at Oxford, after, according to her own account, parting with Sir Charles Dilke in the morning at Warren-street, or when she returned. home from Dublin, where she had passed her time with Captain Forster. A good deal has been made of ir Charles Dilke's snipping out entries from his diary. He cut them out r exclaimed Mrs. Crawford, with a roguish laugh of incredulity, when Sir Charles gave evidence on this point. It is an odd habit, but it is very characteristic. Sir Charles has curious mannerisms about letters and papers. I have frequently watched him whilst sitting on the Treasury Bench dealing with a letter that may have just reached. • him. I have seen him tear out with infinite pains and practised skill a line or two of the writing. This he has tern up an,d thrown in fragment's over the bench behind. Anothersapplication of firm and. nimble fingers-has torn out another slip, the minute fragments of which have been cast at his feet. What was left was a jagged piece of paper very much like the election address held up in court the other day. This was finally disposed of by being torn up. There is a curious rumour about a great marriage in the theatrical world. Strange to sayit is not Mary Anderson. She seems to have been unusually quiet for the last few weeks. Except that she was at the Academy soiree, very little seems to be known about her. She has the same house in the Boltons, and is living with her mother and stepfather, but I have not seen her at any theatre nor heard of her as likely to appear again in the forthcoming season. No bishops areieputed to be engaged to her, and her face has even become something of a rarity in the shop windows. Perhaps she is about to retire on her abundant laurels, or having been too much puffed in past seasons, she will inaugurate a future one by a surprise. The great marriage that is rumoured is great 'from the position of -the bride- groom rather than of the bride. She is a member of Mr. Daly's company, now playing at the Strand, and. he is a son--the eldest son—of Mr. James Gould, the rich American speculator. Then there is another marriage which should have been solemnised long ago, dud is now delayed. Madame Nillson was to be united to Count Casa Misanda. The delay arises from difficulties at the Vatican. She, a fair-haired. daughter of the north, is of course a Protestant. The Count is an Italian and a Roman Catholic, so that the Pope has to be heard in the matter. His Holi- ness has nothing to say against the match, but there ' are delays in getting the dispensation. Maclaine Nillson announces that she will never again appear before a London audience, but those who know her best say she is so great an artist that the applause of the public is the breath of her nostrils. Rubinstein has ret-arned to Russia very rich and bent on composition. He will take as his subject the life of .our Saviour and will compose music, not for a cantata or an oratorio, but for an opera. It' will be as if the Ober-Ammergau play were set to music—only that Rubinstein will deal with the life of the Saviour as interpreted, not by the Latin, but by the Greek Church.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THIJILSDA.Y. There is one circumstance in connection with Mr. Gladstone's lately recurrent resignations of office which is satisfactory from the public busi- ness point of view. They are always accepted with an alacrity that leaves nothing to be desired. When Lord Salisbury has found himself in a simi- lar position he has been summoned to Balmoral. Efforts have been made to induce him to reconsider his decision, and the necessary ultimate summons to Mr. Gladstone has been delayed by applications to Lord Hartington to undertake the task. This time, as heretofore, the proceedings in connection with Mr. Gladstone's resignation have been most busi- ness-like. It was proffered immediately after the meeting of the Council late on Monday afternoon, and early the next Morning Mr. Gladstone received Ithe gracious acceptance of Her Majesty, whilst the I telegraph was invoked to summon Lord Salis- bury from France, 3fr. Gladstone being consider- ately relieved from the trouble involved in the I usual course of personally waiting won Her Majesty to tender his resignation." Thus much is then irrevocably and satisfactorily settled. Mr. t Gladstone has gone out and Lord Salisbury is coming in. But this is only the beginning of the end, an interlude in a drama that can have but one closing scene. One thing Liberals throughout the country will hear with satisfaction; that is, that Mr. Gladstone

is not in any measure personally overwhelmed or depressed by the refusal Of the country, upon the first application, to sanction Home Rule for Ireland. The effect of the repulse has rather been to renew his vigour, and cause him to press more vigorously towards the goal he has convinced himself he will _ _ .

reach before he dies. Achilles will not sulk in his tent, but with his diminished following will yet overcome the allied hosts opposed to him. This extraordinary character was never more curiously developed than now. He takes his defeat with the elation that,with other people, would attend a great success. He is in excellent health, and evenbuoyant spirits. I met him on Tuesday afternoon strolling up Bond-street, arrayed in White waistcoat, white hat, blue necktie, and light trousers. swinging a stick in his hand, and walking with elastic step. I am not sure he was not whistling. The same even- ing he dined out with a friend, and afterwards, arm-in-arm with Mrs. Gladstone, went to the Duke of Westminster's ball, partly to work off the exu- berance of his spirits, and partly to show that there was no malice born of the Duke's unmannerly attack on Mr. Gladstone. The simple fact is that Mr. Gladstone has made up his mind todive to carry the Home Rule scheme with his own hand, and it is wonderful what a man can do in this direction when he tries. Some interest pertains to the question—where will the dissentient Liberal chiefs sit in the new House? Whilst their colleagues were in office this was a matter of course and of easY settlement. When a minister leaves his colleagues during their term of office he invariably takes one of the corner seats on a back bench. In olden times this was a matter absolutely free froth difficulty. It was a notable affair that there should be one • revolted Minister, and there was always room for him on a corner seat. Mr. Forster, after he left his colleagues, naturally took refuge in the corner seat immedi- ately behind the Treasury Bench. This had been appropriate d by Dr. Lyons, then member for Dublin, who found it a convenient coign of vantage for the - delivery of some of his stupendous orations upon things in general. He, for a long time, withstood Mr. Forster's presumption of right to the seat. Mr. Forster, however, had away of literally sitting upon the hon. gentleman, which had its due effect. It was evident he would have the seat whether Dr. Lyons was in it or not. So, after a brief experience, Dr. Lyons took care to be out of it when he saw the burly form of the member for Bradford lurching down the floor of the House. In the single session of the last Parliament mat- ters in this respect grew grievOusly complicated. There were more retired Ministers than there were corner seats. Mr. Bright retained his below the gangway; Mr. Goschen had his above the gangway. Then came Lord llartington, who took the corner seat which Mr. Forster had won, Mr. Goschen hold- ing the one behind. This left only two, and Mr. Dillwyn was immovable from his seat below the gangway, and Mr. Trevelyan only occasionally se- cured the top seat. Sir Henry James and Mr. Chamberlain were left without a special place, and were fain to fall in with the undistinguished rank and file. Where will they go when the parties , change places and the Liberals cross over? Sir Henry James says he will sit on the front Opposi- tion bmch alongside of Mr. Gladstone and the faith- ful remnant of the Ministerial cohort. I don't know whether or not this is said in jest. Sir Henry James would certainly be in his right in taking a place on the front bench, though if his example be followed by Lord Hartington, 'Mr. Chamberlain, Sir George Trevelyan (if he gets a seat), and Mr. Bright it will he rather an awkwardly mixed company. Qne reason that would induce such a course is found in the fact that the Irish members remaining immov- able on the left of the Speaker will not be very agreeable companions for dissentient Liberal chiefs. They may be depended upon to see that neither

div.head: WARRINGTON FARREV CLUB!
div.p: WARRINGTON FARREV CLUB!

A meeting of the memb3rs of this club was held on Wednesday afternoon at the White Ball Inn, Horse- market-street, Warrington. The president, Mr. John Marsh, Grappenhall, occupied the .chair, and there was a fair attendance.—The Clieruersee said that most of them were aware that during the recent heavy rains there had been a oertain amount of damn done by the overflowing of the river Mersey. The crops of some of the members of that club had been damaged, and it had been mooted that there should be something done in the way of 'suing the Bridgewater Trustees for compensation. It was then decided, after some discussion, that a special fund should be raised for the pur- pose of obtaining compensation (rem the Bridgewater Trus- tees, and several substantial contributions towards this fund were promised at the meeting.—Mr. GIBSON said that he did not think there was way clause in the Manchester Ship Canal Company's Act which would make them any more liable than the present Trustees after they had taken 'over khe Bridgewater Canal, so that if they could not make the Trustees liable they would not be able to make the Ship Canal Company liable. Mr. Glbsort also mentioned that he had sustained about £6O worth of damage this year from ovetflows.—Mr. Wieteeet DARBYSRIILE said that within the memory of people living the Bridgewater Company used to pay compensation for damages annually, and he did not see any reason why they should not do that now.—The secre- tary (Mr. Stelfox) was then appointed secretary to the new fund, and the chairman treasurer.—The SECRETARY also mentioned that he had received letters, in reply to the cir- cular sent out by the club to Parliamentary candidates, from Mr. T. H. Twemlow and Mr. B. T. Cotton. These letters were read, and both were on the whole favourable to the objects sought by the club. A letter was read from Mr.. Jenkins, solicitor, Warrington, which contained a warning to farmers against the sellers of spurious artificial manures. It was resolved, on the motion of Mr. Bradford, that Mr. Jenkins should be thanked for his letter. —Mr. Devrrisote then read a paper on "Tithes." His ob- ject, he said, was to show that tithes were it voluntary gift, and were afterwards made compulsory by the State. Hav- ing been established by law, they had a perfect right to re- move them by the same process, and he at considerable length contended that such removal would be ai benefit to agriculturists, upon whom tithes were an unjust burden._ ' He urged that by combination farmers could carry out their wishes in this respect. They could send Ito Parliament men who would either have their wrongs redressed, or make it almost iMDOSSibIe to carry on proper government. If they were wishful that tithes should be abolished, let them at the next election rupport only those who would fight for that abolition. If that was done throughout Great Britain they could demand and receive it.—A discussion followed the reading of the paper.—Mr. Joust DARBISHIRE thought that farmers as a class wanted tithes abolishing. They must never cease agitating to bring about a better state of things, and in- duce the Legislature to wipe off this imposition. He pro- posed a vote of thanks to Mr. Derbyshire for his paper.— This was seconded by Mr. J. Kerowees, supported by the CHAIRMAN, and carried.—lt was also sumgested that a me- morial be prepared on the subject to be forwarded to Parlia- ment.—This was all the business of interest.

John Roberts, held their fourth annual school and chapel anniversary on Wednesday. The school children, to the number of 137, sat down to tea in the ' chapel, and afterwards over 100 adults took tea together. The afternoon proved very wet, but towards evening an ad- journment was made to a large field, kindly lent by Mr. Richardson, where games were enjoyed. On the children retnrning to the chapel they were each regaled with buns. Describing the proceedings in court on Tuesday, a corres- pondent says : —The appearance of Mrs. Crawford bad been anxiously looked forward to every day, but it was not sup- posed that sbe would have been called kefore Mr. Matthews had made his speech. Mrs. Crawford during the trial has been plainly attired in a stone-coloured stuff costume dress, turned up with dark velvet, and a brown straw steeple hat, trimmed up the front with white and black satin. She gave her evidence from the first clearly and without embarrass- ment Occasionally she dropped her eyes and played with her scent bottle lying on the desk before her, but there was never a moment's hesitation in answering or in volunteering confessions outside the questions put. On the contrary, very often in reply to a single question, the witness de- liyereu whole paragraphs of evidence, sentence following sentence fluently, coolly, confidently, and without a break in tae continuity of the recital. After the examination bad proceeded about two hours Mrs. Crawford, who is a lady of apparently robust health, without any previous symptoms of exhaustion, suddenly sat down and seemed about to faint. the court being very hot and close. Water was administered by the usher, and for the rest of the afternoon the witness gave her evidence seated; after a pause of half a minute. Mrs. Crawford's strength was restored. Aftsr the cross- examination began there was occasionally less readiness of reply, especially in the confessions of guilty intrigue with. Captain Forster. Twice with prompt decision Mrs. Craw- ford looked up at the judge and appealed to him as to whether she was obliged to answer certain awkward ques- tions, and in a practical way she at once accepted the poei- tiou when his lordship laid it down. At such times the answers were given with lowered voice, but still with mar- vellously little embarrassment, considering the nature of the admissiona made. fue ebsor hiug interest in the Crawford suit was sustained at high pressure during the earlier portion of Wednesday's sitting, when Mrs. Crawford reappearsd, cl id precisely a. on the preceding days, and took her place in the witness- box. Her unexampled self-composure. says a London cor- respondent, did not desert her for a single instant, but she had frequent recourse to her vinaigrette, which ebe invari- ably carries, as do her two sisters. There was the same un- faltering, clear, steady narration of facts that we listene I to on Tuesday, and there was the same tendency to amplify her testimony--n fact, to make little speeches and running comments upon the naked answer which counsel mougtit to elicit from her. Sir Charles Dilke, as usual, kept his eyes riveted upon her, but by no sign or gesture did be betray the emotions that were working within him. Mrs. Ashton Dilke was not nearly so good a witness as her fresh-faced, bright.coloured sister. Ihe strain of mind consequent upon a sve days' attendance in court has told upon her appearance, and she now looks worn and hageard. he spoke in a tone so low as to be aim,at inaudible, and was fr. quently requested by her eonneel to speak up, but in spite of his entreaties her answers were given almost in a murmur. After finishing she left the court with Mrs Crawford, and did not reappear until half hour after lunch, by which time they hat both recov- ered their accustomed good spirits. Sir Charles laughed for the first time in the course of the trial on Wednesday. That was when a man standing in the court was pointed out resembling him, him, and when one of the witnesses was asked whether that gentleman might not have been the ptrson she saw goirg into Warren-street.

PR ESCOT. PRRSCOT SCHOOL BOARD.—The monthly meeting of this Board &mulct have been held on Monday evening, but a quorum of members did not attend. There were only pre- sent Mess's. W. L. Evans and W. Goldsvrorth, with tbo clerk, Mr. H. Cross. The only business was to order the schools to b 3 closed on the following Friday for a month's midsummer holidays. FUNERAL OF THE LATE M. BracKwELL —The remains of the late Mr. Jam-s Blackwell, assistant magistrates' Clerk for the Prescot Division, whose death we reported last week, were interred in the burial ground attached to the Prescot Parish Church, on Saturday afternoon. The funeral was attended by a large number of the members of the Loyalty Lodge of Freemasons (Prescot), of which de- ceased was junior warden; a large number of the local Forresters' Club, and a number of the members of the Royal Bowling Club. The funeral service was conducted by the curate, the Rev F. R. Lee.

Bright, five rough-looking lads were charged with stealing a quantity of fruit, value 5-4, from the garden of Mr. David Hollins, Mosley Hill, Wavertrea, on the 18th mat; they were further charged with stealing a tame rabbit, value 105, the property of Charles Henry Hollins. Evans, Parker, and McDonald were each fined 103 and ordered to ply the value of the articles stolen ; and Barrow and Bitrununs each of whom bas been previ.,usly convicted, were sentenced to three months' imprisonment with bard labour.

div.head: VACCINATION.-AN ANIDIATHD DISCUSSION.
div.p: VACCINATION.-AN ANIDIATHD DISCUSSION.

The Centex read a letter from Mr. Cooper, vaccination officer, Earlestown, in which the names of several defaulters in the matter of vaccination were mentioned, and asking for authority to prosecute the same. Mr. Cooper mentioned that these persons had been previously prosecuted, hut not in respect of the same children.—Mr. HEATON inquired if the children for %Them the persons named had been previ- ouelv prosecuted had been vaccinated.—Mr. CLARKE said be thought he might speak to that. He did not think these children bad been vaccinated, and his impression was that to prosecute such Men only created sympathy and unpleasantness. It seemed strange that Earlestown should be selected by the Local Government Board—not by that Board, for he came there fortnight after fortnight and saw those unpleasant letters coming from the Lecel Government Board, while be could name many towns that were not disturbed at this time. Those mon had been prosecuted Wore, and he dare sly that if they prosecuted them a dozen times they would certainly be worse off in nurse hut no further advanced in regard to vaccination. He there- fore moved that the.e men be not prosecuted.—Mr. HARRI- SON: T Rupeese these are the men who still remain obdu- rate with regard to vaccination.—Mr. Ceaneen said he might say that it was not from any vindictive motives that these men did not get their children vaccinated, but from other curies known to themselves.—Mr. HARRISON: Downright obstinecv.—Mr. CLARKE: No, it is not.—Mr. Beeexnueuter thought they might quietly leave that matter alone.—Mr. Gmsoer said he would second Mr. Clarke's motion that these persons he not prosecuted again —Mr. BROWN moved that the law be followed and that these children be vaccinated. He thought they were hound to do that, and to provide for the safety of the neighbourhood independent of the indivi- dual opinion of these persons.—Mr. HARRISON could not say that he seconded that proposal with pleasure, because he regretted it Was necessary. It did appear to him to be a piece of obstinacy, and downright fanaticism when people were found in these days opposing one of the most beneticient Acts of Parliament— an Act of Parliament which had been proved to be most efficacious in destroying the effects of one of the most loathsome diseases that humanity could be affected with. He did not know whether it was obstinacy or net, but he could only impute it to something of that kind. At any rate it was their duty to follow the law se long as the law existed, and a. long as he was a member of that Board of Guardians he would not encourage law breaking. There- fore he thought their duty was plain ; these people must be taught that they could not have their own way and set the law at defiance.—The CHAIRMAN suagested that Mr. Clarke should move a negative to the proposal of Mr. Brown.—Mr. CLARKS having done this, it was seconded by Mr. HAT- CLIFF.—Mr. HEATON asked if there was not an instruction from the Poor law Board that a person should not be pro- secuted repeatedlv.—The CLERK said that that order did not refer to such cases as they had before them that meet- ing. but to cases where a person had been prosecuted once in respect to a child it left it to their discretion whether he should be repeatedly prosecuted in respect of the same child. It was one of those things that should be exereieed with moderation, the Local Government Board thought, but he might tell them that be had never yet advised a second prosecution in respect of the same child, and they had never done it. In the present Cases, how- ever, they were other children of persons who haat bees prose- cuted.—Mr. RATCLIFFE said he did not think that any per- son in Earlestown would object to be brought before the marristrates once. but it was these repeated prosecutions that were objected to. They were very much obliged to Mr. Brown for his sympathy with Earlestown, and he would be glad if Mr. Brown would visit the place and see it for himself. He (Mr. Ratcliffe) had seen men as respectable as the mayor (Mr. Harrison) himself refuge to have their children vaccinated, and they did not do this from any vin- dictive motives, or to further any interest of their own.— Mr VOISEY soggested that they should let the matter drop. But if it was put to the vote he should be compelled to vote that the law be carried out. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Beeex• HURST agreed with Mr. Voisey, and thought it would be unfortunate if it went to the public that they had definitely decided not to prosecute people a second time —Mr. GREEN- ING said he must confess that he was not a very strong be- liever in vaccination, and he bad seen certain matters which confirmed him that he ought not to be a very strong believer in it, whatever Mr. Harrison might say on the sub- ject. He ('sir. Greening) could instance things that had come under his own observation—and he thought they had had one the previous day at the committee, which to him was a most horrible piece of business. It was not all medi- cal men in the world that agreed with vaccination. There was a doctor in the town who said in his house some years ago that if he had 20 children he would not have one of them vaccinated; be would sell, be said, the bed from under hint to pay the fines rather than that one of them should be vaccinated. He considered, as a medical man, that vaccination was an abomination. That was only one man he (Mr. Greening) admitted, but be was a man of high education and great attainments in his profession, and that was his opinion. If that matter came to a vote, be should keep his seat and not vote either way.—Mr. CLARICE said that 90 per cent of the people did not object to vaccination, but to compulsory vaccination.—Mr. JOLLEY said that was a question of law or no law, and he should support the lawe The CHAIRMAN said that as long as it was law he did not see how they could be justified in not carrying it out. Ha thought the proper thing to do was to tackle the law.—Mr. Gietsoet said he believed the Oldham Guardians had stopped prosecuting in cases which had been prosecuted before Mr. CLARKE : In Leicester they have stopped all prosecu- tions —Mr. HARRISON : They cannot stop prosecutions.—Mr. CLARE: They have.—Mr. HARRISON: Do you mean to tell me that the Leicester Guardians can ignore the law ?—Mr. CLARKE : Thee have; I can suhetantiate tey statement.— The CLERK here suggested that as there seemed to be a division of opinion On the Board, that he should ask the advice of the Local Government Board. He mentioned that this vaccination difficulty arose in Earlestown only. /f the people were free in Warrington he did not think they would have any difficulty. It was purely an Earlestown difficultv.—Mr. HARRISON : Yes, some pedagogue set it goirg there, and it has spiced since.—Mr. RATCLIFFE : Let Mr. Plarrieon withdraw that remark. (Laughter.)—The clerk's euggestion that the Local Government Board should be applied to for advice was then agreed to.

div.head: FOUND DROWNED AT WALTON.
div.p: FOUND DROWNED AT WALTON.

On Wednesday afternoon a carter named Forshaw saw the body of a man ftoating on the river Hersey, near Walton Arches, which, on being removed to the Sta.4's Head Inn, Walton Inferior, was found to be that of a man named William Rownds, 40 years of age, a csrtar by occupation, who had been missing from his borne since the previous Friday. Deceased had lived at 49. Wilderspool-road, and leaves a widow and three children. Be left home on Friday morn- ing to bring back ssme tools from where he had been working as a labourer, and said that he should be home to dinner. He did not, however, do so, and bills were issued asking for information and giving a descriprion„ Nothing was heard of him until For- shaw and another person saw the body in the water. They had taken shelter from the rain underneath the Walton Arches, and saw something at one side of the water, near the bank. They went to the place and saw that it was the body of a man. Or Thursday afternoon Mr. Worsley, coroner (Ridgway and Worsley), held as inquiry into the death at the Stag's Head Inn,—Mary Rownde, widow of the deceased, said that ber h-sb,Fd was a carter. He had been out of work for some the,, but worked on odd days when he could get it. She last saw him at 9-30 on the previous Friday morning, when he said be was going to Lung bits tools home from the place where he had been working. He said that he should be back to dinner, but did not come. He had lost his appe- tite, and had suffered from loss of sleep for a few nights. He was always very cheerful in disp,sition. She never knew him to be subjecc to fainting. Deceased was very hapi.,v at home, and if he was short of work witness was able to keep the house going by her own earnings. She never saw him after he left home. In answer to a jurymen, witness said that her husband was not addicted to orinking; he only sp,nt say is. or is. 61 a week le that way. On the Monday morning, after he did not return home, she issind bills advertiting for him. —John Forshaw, Warrington, a carter, was the next witness. He said that on Wednesday afternoon at but three o'clr ck he saw the body of the deceased floating in the river Mersey at Walton Inferior. He assisted in re- covering the body, which was much decomposed, and brought it to the Stag Inn. With, ss knew the deceas, d, who was a very decent fellow to work with. Witness had not •ieen him for some months and did not know that he was de- pri s4ed in spirita —P.C. Bennett, of the Cheshire Conetabu- lars, stati ned at Walton, said that he had examinid the oody and found no marks of violence upon it.—Tbe Coroner ud that the police had made enquiries as to anyone who had seen the deceased after he was miosed, but there was no evidence to show how he came by his death.—The jury re- turned an open verdict that the deceased was founddrownad.

div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at Union Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday forenoon, when there were present—Mr. J. Lowe (chairman), Rev. Father Finegan. Mesars. William Tyrer, J. Matthews, W. Gerrard, J. Jackson, W. G. Ashton, J. Buckley, W. Burchall, J. Burch4ll, C. B. Johnson, J. Fisher, T. Eatock, J. Griffiths, J. Kenwright, J Ranson, J. W. Wareing, E. yder, P. Middiehurat, J. Whalley, R. Tuson, T. F. Hill, J. Leatherbarrow, H. Hulnae, W. thane, and S. H. Hartley (clerk.) -Twat' RELIEF COMMITIEES —The Local Government Board wrote on 20th July enclosing orders rescinding pre- vious orders with respect to the IToion Relief Committees, and makiqg further provision with regard to the appoint- ment of district committees t) deal with applications for relief and the payment of school fees. The Clerk said it would be necessary for the Guardians to make arrangements for carrying out the orders, and they must_ fix the places for the meetings. He had hoped the relief office at St.. Helens would have been sufficient for the purpose, but it was for the Guaidiens to consider whether they had sufficient accom- modation. The same thing would apply to Widnes.. He thought they should have ante-rooms,. so that applicants would not necessarily hear each other's applications fee relief. He suggested that he should confer with the Guar- dians ef the respec!ive districts and report upon the matter at tbe next meeting of the Board.:—Mr.. Gerrard seid such a;place was greatly wanted at Widnes. It was too far tor the poor people to have to come there (to the Workhouse —Mr. Hill asked if there was anything in the order which would clash with the duties of the local School Attendance Committees —The Clerk said there was not.—After some further discussion, the cletk's suggestion was adopted. THFI WOOLTON ASSISTANT OVERSEER —The Clerk re- ported the receipt of the bond for £l,OOO, as surety for Mr. Beater, the newly-appointed Resistant overseer for Wootton. The bond was referred to the Finance Committee. NB. BARTON'S SALARY: INCREASE ORANTED.—In accor- dance with notice of motion given at the last meeting, Mr. Jackson moved that the salary of Mr. 0. M. Barton, re- lieving officer for the Eccleston district, be increased from £lOO to £l2O per annum. He said the matter had been frequently diecussed on previous occasions, and he had little to add. When he last appealed to them he (Mr. Jackson) said Mr. Barton had six children, but ha had, un- fortunately, seven of a family, and not one bringing him in a penny.—Mr. W. Birchen seconded the motion, and said Mr. Barton bad always been a very good and efficient officer. He was qoite deserving of the increase.—Mr. C. B. Johnson held the opinion that it was desirable a minority should cheerfully acquiesce in the decisions of the inajority, and after the majority had decided to postpone the consid- eration of the application he thought they should abile with the resolution.—Mr. Daine agreed with Mr Johnson, and he had heard no additional reasons why they should now grant the application. It would be treating the Board with discourtesy to ask them to again vote upon a resolution which was before them six weeks ago. He proposed an amendment that the subject be not discussed.— Mr. Tyrer said the resolution postponing the application on the former occasion was only passed by a majority of one, and it would not have been carried had it not seen for the attendance on that occasion of an ex-officio member who did not often attend their meetings.—Mr. Daine : There Is always an "if "about. it.—Mr. Ranson supported Mr. Jack- son's proposition, and Mr. Kenwright seconded the amend- ment.—The increase, according to the resolution of Mr. Jackson—was ultimately granted by 18-votes to 3. THE ST. HELENS- CORPORATION AND THE The Clerk reported that since the last meeting he had had an interview with the Health Committee of the St. Helens Corporation regarding the admission of pauper patients to the St. Helens Infectious- Diseases Hospital. The Corpora- tion were of opinion that the Guardians should pay 44 6,1 per day per patient for their maintenance in that institution, and in addition pay the cost of removal of patients from their homes to the hospital. The Corporation originally asked Ss per day, and the Guardians thought 34 per day sufficient. The Corporation had therefore divided the amount. As vet, not a single pauper case had been sent into that hospital ;. and he had pointed out to the committee that the amount the Guardians expended on St. Helens paupers was £2OOO. a year more than what was paid by the St. Helena ratepamers.— Mr. J. Leatherharrow moved that the Guardians adhere to their former eft\-r to pay 3s per day for each patient, and Mr. Buckley seconded the motion.—Mr. J. Burch4ll said if the Guardians had to remove patients from tat. Helens to the Workhouse it might interfere with the healtbs of the patients,, and he suggested the Guardians should try Ps meet the St. Helens Cerporation in a generous spirit.—The Clerk said the Guardians contended that they ought not to pay anything towards the establishment charges of the St. Helens hospi'al —Mr Wareing asked what was the actual cost of maintenance of each patient.—The Clerk re- plied that it was is 8d per day, and the Guardians had offered to pay 3s.—rhe motion was then passed. This was the principal business.

THE ALLEGED PRIZE FIGHT AT BURTON WOOD.

On Wednesday afternoon Messrs. J. Rylancls and Z. Armitage were engaged a considerable time at the Sessions-room in Irlam-street, inquiring into, the particulars of a prize fight alleged to have taken place at Burtonwood on the afternoon of Saturday, the 19th of June, James Lewis and Edward Scott, young men, were charged by the police with com- mitting a breach of the peace by fighting a prize fight at Buttonwood, and thirty-three men and youths were charged with aiding and abetting. Mr. P. Davies appeared for the defendants. The case for the police was that on the Saturday in question. shortly after noon, a match was arranged between Lewis and Scott, the stakes to be aside. That arrangement was made at Earlestown, and it was decided to bring off the encounter at Burtonwood. The other men summoned were those who were present watching the fight.. The money was duly staked and on arrival at Burtonwood the two prin- cipals stripped, and men named James Coleman and Henry Crowder, both living in the neighbourhood of Earlestown, acted as seconds. Time was taken , in the way adopted at prize fights.. One witness stated that when one of the men was knocked down, time was called, and he was picked up by his second. Coleman acted for Lewis and Crowder for Scott.. The two , princi- pals fought from forty to forty-seven rounds,. when, an alarm of police being raised, the fight was stopped. After hearing evidence for the. prosecution the two magistrates consulted together,. and said that the evidence bore out a contention. submitted by Mr. Davies that the affair was not in. the strict sense of the word a prize fight. The stakes, it had been stated, had not been awarded to either combatant. They should treat the cases an ordinary breach of the peace by binding over the defendants to be of good behaviour for six. months. —Mr. Davies pointed out that some of those who had been summoned were merely casual onlookers, and stated that others summoned were not,. in fact, near Burtonwood at the time the fight was alleged to have taken place. After a little discussion and inquiry the Bench decided that the principals and those defendants who had come with them, from Earlestown, and .also seemed to be connected with the affair, should be bound over. They were also ordered to pay costs. After defendants had been so bound over Mr. Davies said that he should never have conSented to such a course hadhe known that the costs were what they were stated to be. The total costs for those bound over, fifteen number, amounted to over £lO. BY this, he said, he had been taken unawares, and wished. the de-- tailed figures to be supplied him. There were many amongst the defendants who could not have been found guilty. Mr. Rylands said that if there was anything wrong he had no doubt that it would be put right. Mr. Davies said that he never dreamt that the costs would be £lO 2s 6d for a paltry case of that kind. The matter then dropped.

div.head: PRECOT HORTICULTURAL SOCIETY.
div.p: PRECOT HORTICULTURAL SOCIETY.
ANNUAL EXHIBITION.

The second annual exhibition of the Prescot and' District Horticultural Society was held on Thursday afternoon in a field at Parkside, kindly lent for the occasion by Par. W. L. Evans, J.P. The society was established about two years ago for the encourage- ment of cottage gardening among the working classes, and it has had a most successful career. Last year's show was on a small scale and was held in the Crown Hotel. There were then only to exhibitors, who competed for prizes anaounting in value to £7, while on the present occasion no less a sum than £45 was offered in prizes, and there were 35 .exhibitors. The society is energetically ntanageo. by Mr. George Rigby, president ; Mr. Eugene McCarthy, vice. president; Mr. Joseph Rainford, treasurer; and Mr. Robert Rigby, secretary; who have been ably assisted by a strong committee.

-Unfortunately the weather was of a most unfavourable character at the time of opening, and there was a heavy shower of about an hour's duration. The exhibits were neatly arranged and stigsd in a spacious marquee supplied by Mr. Owen Price, of Wigan' who also erected the refresh- ment and secretary's tents. The judeing and awarding 01 the prizes was a difficult task, but it was•eaeisfactortly per- formed by Mr. Stevenson, heart gardener to Lieutenant- Colonel W. W. Pilkington, J.P., of the Hazels, Preecot ; Mr. Edeard Bridge, of Huvton, gardener to Mr. Jewett, and secretary to the Sault Horticultural Society ; and Mr. Durant, gardener to Mr. W. L. At the County Asylum, Rainhill, on Wednesday, Mr. Brighouse. held an inqnest on the body of Thos. Lyon, a pauper patient, who on Monday threw him- s.-/f from a halcmy 18ft. high, and alighting on bill head received such injuries that death ensued shortly afterwards. At the request o/ the Coroner, the meal' cal superintendent (Dr, Rogers) conducted the jail to t}:s ba'cony in question. The inquest WM subsequently held in the boardroom.—Dr. Hickson, aes;etant medical imperiatthdent, tinted that deceased was admitted on the 9th June on a magistrate's order He was a glass polisher and had lodged at Collier's-square, Sutton. On the 10th ult. deceased picked 80171 a glass from a conservatory win' dow and got through. He went to come friends and ob.' tained clothing, and then went to Wigan.- He was brought back on the 11th ult. Decease I was under the constant care of an attendant. No patients were allowed on that bal- cony without an attendant. The balcony was used to cross_ from No. 4 ward to No. 2" ward, two separate biocks of- buildings. Dr. Rogers and witness saw the man as he lay. in the yard. He had sustained fracture of the skull and injury to his brain. If the door badbeen locked the acth. dent would not have happened.—The Coroner : Has titer! been any inquiry by the visiting justices ?--Dr• Rogers I reported it to the justices who were then sitting, out they left it ever until after the inquest. It will c,,nle , bad them at the next meeting.—Dr. Hickson said. he had W Attendant Neii to take special charge of deceased, and not allow him more than an arm's length away at any Harry Woodhouse Neil (attendant), said be had been an at- t.ndarit seven weeks, and bad not any previous enlerie"e in asylum work He remembered Dr. Hickson giving hint orders not to allow deceased more than an arm's length frr him. He admitted his vigilance was !int ei4thSee so. sharp at that moment, but Me really thought .-- balcony door was leck,d and that deceased was safe' A Juryman said be naught the attendant felt he was doinq his duty. His statement was very straightforward.---Chiel A-ttendant James Grey said he was at the doer 01 No• Ward w)ten deceased came along. Neil was ten or twelve. yards behind him. Witness shouted to him to take deceas:c; down to the airing court. Deceased turned round, walk three sr four yards, anti then vaulted over the coping on teet the cornice. Neil caught deceased's coat, but could no hold, aro deceased fell below.—Attendast Iboadley plainer' that it was his custom when he but turned the men out of the wards inv the airing court to open the bo,loonS' door and allow air to go into No. 2 ward. The men etmoke! in that place, and witness had been told to open the balonng door to•let in fresh air. If he had thought Lyon was ing irro the ward he would have locked the docre--14' Rogets cold in consequence of alterations and additions t.n. the building, they were in a state of confusion, and'al though he bad taken every precaution to prevent accidentst he•felt-ittgaid that something might occur. He could on` say be gave the order for the door to be opened, bet,". thought the attendant was ri4ht in opening Coroner said the attendants had very onerous duties to Pet, form. and they could only do them to the best of the" ability ;: they could not perform miracles.—The jury' thheing. returned a verdict to the effect that decease I met with "- death acoid, ntally whilst attempthg t.) escape from the asylum; and no blame was attributable to anyone.

HE WAS DETERMINED TO MAKE MATTERS SE.—ln the Southern States of America, prior to the Rebellion, bloodhounds were kept to pursue runaway slaves who took refuge in the swamps, and also to hunt convicts. Orders Were issued to the Northern troops during the campaign to kill all these animals as they were met with. On one occa- aiOn a soldier picked up a poodle, the favourite pet of its Mistress, and was carrying it off to execution, when the lady Made a strong appeal to him to spare it. The soldier re- plied, "Madam, our orders are to kill every bloodhound." "But this is not a bloodhound," said the lady. " Well, eoadam, we cannot tell what it will grow irto if we leave it behind !" rejoined the soldier, as he went cif with it. A Germaii petsant-f amity had made all their arrangements to emigrate to the United Stetes. The day before the family was to t dee their departure the eldest son, Hans, who Vas an enormous eater, intimated that he did not care to go West. "Has some village maiden beguiled thee to remain behind ?" asked the father. "Nothing of the kind.' "Why, then, dost thou not wish to go with us ?" "I have been telking to the schoolmaster, and--" "Well, what did he lay ?" "He say", when it Is twelve &clock with us here in Germany, that—" "That what ?" "Weer] it is twelve O'clock here with u, in America it is nine o'clock in the evening." e Well?" "I don't want to go to a place where I have to wait that long for my dinner !" And leans broke down at the mere thought of it. PLAYING DUMMY—Jones was sauntering about at the Academy recently, and chanced to meet a friend, a deaf- mute, who was oonversing with a companion in sign- language. Greeting Jones cordially, the deaf mute drew Out a pocket pad and pencil, and, after a brief pencil-and- Paper conversation, introduced his companion by the same means, and shortly after withdrew. Jones and the stranger discussed the pictures pleasantly for twenty minutes or more, reeanwhile covering the backs of sundry envelopes and scraps of Raper with their pencilling% when a fourth Character in this little drama came upon tho scene—a friend of Jones's new-made acquaintance. Hallo, George !" said the dumb man to the new-comer familiarly. "How do you like the pictures this year ?" "By Jupiter!" exclaemed Jones, in surprise. "Can you talk ?" " Well, I should say so," said the gentleman, equally surprised, as he suddenly Put away perci: and paper. "Anent you deaf an,i (lamb "Not by a good deal," Jones replied, thrusting into his Docket an envelope nearey covered with penciemarks ; "brit I'll kill dummy next time I meet him !"

div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

The following interesting account of the Man- chester Ship Canal accompanies two capital bird's- eye views in "The Illustrated London News" for Saturday last. One illustration covers the course from Liverpool_ to Warrington, and the other from

Warrington to Manchester; In February, 1883, we published a full description of the leading features of the projected Manchester Ship Canal, accompanied by a bird's-eye view of its whole course, with plans of the docks and other illustrations of this grand undertaken.% At that time the promoters were on the eve of the com- mencement of a prolonged and costly series of Par- liamentary conflicts, extendins. over four sessional campaigns; the proceedings of the Six Parliamen- tary Select Committees occupied 175 days, during which 543 examinations of witnesses were made, and no less than 87,936 questions were put and answered. The Manchester Ship Canal Act (48 and 49 Vic. cap. 118) received the Royal Assent on August Vic., 1885. The Act incorporates the Man- chester Ship Canal Company for two principal ob- jects, and for other purposes :-1. To construct a ship canal from the deep water of the Mersey Estu- ary, at Eastham, near Liverpool, by way of Elles- mere Port, Weston Point, and Runcorn, to Warring- ton, Salford, and Manchester, for the largest ocean steamers, with docks at Manchester, Salford,' and Warrington, and other incidental works. 2. To purchase the entire interest of the Bridgewater Navigation Company, Limited, the price of which is fixed by the Act at £1,710,000. The Bridgewater Navigation system includes the Bridgewater Canals. the Runcorn and Weston Canal, the Mersey and Irwell Navigation, the Runcorn Docks, and the Duke's Dock at Liverpool, with wharves, ware- houses, lands, and buildings. The, authorised share capital of the Manchester Ship Clenal Company is £8,000,000, with borrowing powers to the extent of £1,812,000, making the total authorised capital £9,812,000: a sum sufficient to enable the Com- pany to comp,lete the cOnstruction of the works, to psy interest during their constructiOn, alld to carry into effect all the objects of the Act, and to leave an ample surplus. A further bill authorising the payment by the Manchester Ship Canal Company of interest at the rate of 4 per cent. per annum to shareholders during the construction of the works, became law, and received the Royal Assent as an Act of Parliament on June 26th, 1886. Messrs. Lucas and Aird have entered into a con- tract with the Company to construct the entire works authorised, in four years, for the sum of £5,750,000, or £561,137 under the engineer's esti- mate. Ship canals are now engaging the attention of capitalists in various parts of the world, owing much to the great success of the Suez Canal. It is clear that a large water-, ay, over which steamers of great capacity can pass, affords the readiest and much the cheapest mode of transit. Water is the only medium on which traffic can pass without wear and tear; and • heavy cost of maintenance. Railways, tramways, and roads of every descrip- tion deteriorate in the same ratio as the weight of traffic carried over them; and large water-ways alone possess the great advantage of being able to double or treble their traffic Without any appreci- able increased cost of repair. In fact, the Suez Canal doubled its traffic while the working ex- penses remained almost stationary, notwithstanding that it was originally constructed of a width of only 78 ft. at bottom, which necessitates passing places and detention of traffic at those points The engineers of the Manchester Ship Canal (Mr. James Abernethy and Mr. E. Leader Williams) have de- signed that work with a minimum bottom width of 120 ft., which will enable the largest class of steam- ers to pass at any point, In actual working, how- ever, this will rarely occur, as steamers leaving Manchester will be out of the Canal and in the Mer- sey, near Liverpool, before the large inward-bound steamers have entered the Canal. The necessity for large steamers passing over the bar at the mouth of the Mersey at or near high water will so regulate the traffic, that largAessels will, as a rule, pass each other in the Mersey between the Canal en- trance locks at Eastham and the sea. Another point in which the Manchester Ship Canal differs from the Suez Canal is in having locks to raise the shipping using the Canal from. the sea level to the level of the quays of the Man- chester and Salford Docks, a rise of about 60 feet. M. Lesseps, no doubt, exercised a wise discretion, in constructing the Suez Canal without locks. The seas he joined, were practically on one level, the sand excavation was easy, and cheap labour was abundant. The rise of tide in the Suez Canal is slight, and does not interfere With navigation. How far he has been wise in adopting the same course for the Panama Canal remains yet to be seen. Most of his difficulties in the construction of that work have arisen through his not adopting locks, and it appears probable they must yet be re- sorted to before the Canal is made. The ship canals to Amsterdam and to Ghent have'both been lately constructed, and with locks, and not the slightest difficulty has arisen in navigating those canals. Hardly a dock in the world is without an entrance lock; and the Manchester Ship Canal will virtually be a series of four long docks joined by locks. The advantage thus gained will be very considerable. Goods will be delivered at once at quay level. Steamers navigating the Canal above Warrington will be out of all tidal currents and in slack water. Side docks or lay-byes can be formed at any points without gates or expensive entrances, and there- fore shipping will always load or discharge with great facility. The cost of the work will be largely reduced by the adoption of locks, and therefore the Company will be able to charge low tolls for the use of the Canal. In fact the maximum tolls that can be levied under the Act are about half the present charges for carriage and dock dues. These tolls, owing to the low cost of maintenance of the Canal, will secure a highly remunerative return to in- vestors. The district through which the Manchester Ship Canal passes is rich in mineral and great industries. At Widnes and Runcorn there are large chemical works, while St. Helens is near and is united by canal to the Mersey. At Warrington the ironworks are on a large scale, and a great weight of wire and other goods is yearly exported. The docks at Weston Point are joined to the great Cheshire salt- field, by the Weaver Navigation, over which a mil- lion tons of salt passes per annum for exportation. At Runcorn, the Ship Canal Company will be the owners of the Bridgewater Docks, which are con- nected with the Staffordshire potteries and coal and iron industries by the Trent and Mersey and Bridge- water Canals. At Partington and Bartoe, the Wigan and Worsley coal-fields are only a few miles from the Ship Canal, to which they will be joined by existing railway and canal systems. The Parting- ton coal basin will be only about thirty miles from the Yorkshire coal-field, which at present has no available outlet on the west coast. At Manchester the docks will be on a large scale, with several miles of quays, with ample shed accommodation. These docks are close to the great railway systems, and are united to the River Irwell, from which canals proceed through Yorkshire, Cheshire, and Staffordshire, which districts will be largely bene- fitted by the ship Canal. Nowhere, in or out of , England, is there such a population and such an amount of trade, and there can be little doubt that much of it will be absorbed by the Ship Canal. Along its banks will be centred the great factories of the future. The facility with which imported materials will be at once moved fr nu shipping without further carriage or break of bulk into manufactories and works, and reshipped when re- quired, must give an advantage to Lancashire trade which it will not be slow to develop, and which will react on the country generally. It is understood that the contractors will lay thirty-five miles of railway along the route of the Canal, to expedite the progress of the works, and will have upon the lines 3,000 waggons worked by eighty locomotives. The works will be carried on continuously by day and by night, with relays of labour, and will involve the employment of seme- thing like 20,000 men. In order to facilitate the night work, the works Will be illumined by the electric light. The contract being in the hands of so capable a firm as Messrs. Lucas and Aird, who have successfully executed some of the most exten- sive works in the world, is a sufficient guarantee that the Canal will be completed within the appoin- ted time; so that by the middle of 1890, thanks to the persistent energy of Mr. Daniel Adamson and his colleagues, Manchester will be able to enter upon a new and important development, and will ere long add to her other distinctions that of being one of the great ports of the world. There can be no question that, allowing for a few years' opera- tion of the Ship Canal, Manchester, as the commer- cial emporium of a district which, it can be estab- lished, is concerned to the extent of 60 per cent of the entire foreign trade of England and Wales, is bound to make-her mark among the sea havens of the world. The port of Liverpool, whose traffic mainly depends upon the Manchester district, has more than seven times the volume of traffic required to make the Manchester Ship Canal a financial suc- cess. In answer to those who contend that it will not pay, the Duke of Bridgewater's canal, more
