Ithan a century ago, and the Manchester and Liver- pool Railway, were met with the same objection_ The fact that the Manchester Ship Canal will afford the most convenient accommodation for large steamers over an area of 7,500 square miles, with a: population of 7,000,000, is sufficient to establish the financial prosperity of this great enterprise. From the balcony of the great tower of that pala- tial municipal edifice, the Manchester Town Hall, a commanding view might be obtained, if the atmo- sphere were clear, of the entire route of the Man- chester Ship Canal, from its commencement at East- ham to its terminus, • about a mile from the Manchester Royal Exchange. Looking in a direction generally west by south, one might see, lying almost at the foot of the tower, the extensive series of docks and wharf- age accommodation, eitendinc, from what is known as Woden-street foot-bridge to Barton-upon-Irwell, a distance of between three or four miles. In the Manchester and Salford Docks alone there will be three miles of lineal quay frontage, in addition to about six miles of quays fronting the river between Manchester and Barton-upon-Irwell. Along these quays, hundreds of vessels will find accommoda- tion. _

Extending our vision to the outer extremity of the harbour of Manchester at Barton, we should see the Bridgewater Canal crossing the line of the Ship Canal; this will be effected by an aqueduct, crossing at the same level as tile original aqueduct, constructed with two spans, one of which will con- sist of a caisson or trough, which will be moveable on a centre; like an ordinary swing bridge. The end of the trough, and of the aqueduct upon which the trough closes, will be provided with water- tight gates, to prevent the escape of water while ; the trough i s turned. At Barton there will be one of the sets of locks and sluices. At this point there will also be barge-lifts and coal-tips, so that traffic can be transferred direct into the barges from one canal to the other, or coal can be tipped direct from boats into the ship. Looking a little further, we perceive another set of 19cli.s and sluices, at Ham; and on the left bank of the canal, just below the Irlam locks, the Ship Canal will receive the accession of the waters of the Mersey, this being the point of the confluence !of the Irwell and the Mersey. On the same side of the river, and just below the p )int; last mentioned, is Partington, where there will be a basin for load- ing coal from high-level tips, with branch railways connecting the Ship Canal with the system of the Cheshire Lines Committee. Provision will thus be made for a large trade in coal. Again, extending our range of view from Parting- ton to Latchford, a distance of about six miles, there,will be the last set of the series of locks, by which vessels will be raised from the level of the ordinary tidal portions of the canal to the level of the docks at Manchester. _ .

The next point of interest is the Warrington Dock, which branches from the Ship Canal about a mile and a half below the Latchford locks. It will be a commodious dock, being about twenty- five acres in extent of water area. At Warrington, the Ship Canal will be connected with branch rail- ways with the London and North-Western and the Great Western Railway sy.stems. Runcorn, about seven miles below the Warrington Dock, is the next important point on the route. Besides the Runcorn Docks and other properties, the Ship Canal will be at this point connected with the London and North-Western Railway, the Run- corn and Weston Canal, the Runcorn and Latchford Canal, and, via the river Mersey, with the town of Widnes and the Sankey Navigation. Immediately below Runcorn are the Weston Point Docks and the Weaver Navigation, with which the Ship Canal will be connected, Five miles below Weston Point, the Ship Canal will pass in front of Ellesmere Port, where it will be connected with the Shropshire Union Canals and with the London and North-Western and Great Western Railway systems. Three miles further on, at East- ham, will be the tidal gates of entrance to the Ship Canal. These will be worked as locks, at low water, so that large vessels can enter and leave at almost any state of the tide, instead of only during forty minutes at each tide, as at Liverpool. The sill of the largest entrance lock will have 10ft. greater depth of water over it than the deepest entrance at Liverpool. Small vessels will be able to enter and leave at any time. Vessels will navigate the Manchester Ship Canal, with safety, at a speed of five miles an hour; and it is estimated that the passage from the entrance at Eastham to Manchester will be accomplished in eight hours, which is much less time than is now taken to cart goods from ship to rail in Liverpool, and to carry them by rail to Manchester. A large pore will be created in Manchester, which will be more than thirty miles nearer to the great manu- facturing districts of Lancashire, to the West Rid- ing of Yorkshire, and to Cheshire, Staffordshire, and Derbyshire. Foreign produce, Irish, Scotch, and other merchandise brought by the coasting traffic, will be delivered direct into the greatest consuming district of England, probably the greatest in the world. Manchester is not only the centre of the cotton trade, but it has also very large provision, corn, cattle. and fish markets. Large quantities, however, of the provisions, corn, and timber con- sumed in the Manchester district, though sold in the Manchester markets, are stored at the ports of Liverpool, Fleetwood, Hull, Grimsby, Goole, and West Hartlepool. The cost and loss of time in trans-shipment, and in the transit from those ports to :Manchester, cripples the trade of the district, and imposes a heavy burden on the public, which will be relieved by the Manchester Ship Canal.

WIMBLEDON RIFLE MEETING.—The second stage of the Queen's Prize was c mpleted at Wimbledon on Saturday. Captain Cortis, of the 2nd Sussex, carried off the .ilver medal with a score of 194. He tied with Private Jackson, of Grimshy—the 15th Lincolnshire—but in shooting off Curtis scored a bullseye, mire, and inner against three outers recorded by Jackson. Cortis was Sdver Medalist in 1872. In ebe hundred who will scoot in this final stage of the Queen's Prize on Tuesday Lancashire has seven and Cheshire five representatives. The Prince of Wales's Prize was won by Sergeant Gaudin, of the Ist Jersey Militia. The China Cup goes to Shropshire, and the Bel- gian Challenge Cup for ' volley firing to the Ist Westmorland. At the service held in the camp on Sunday the sermon was preached by Canon Hole. Mr. Thomas Tur- ner stands for the Arthur prize with 10 builseyes at 100 yards The chief event of the Wimbledon R,fie Meeting—deciding who should be Queen's Prizeman for the year—was inclu- ded in Wednesday's programme. Three men tied with ag- gregates of 265 points, viz., Private Jackson, Ist Lincoln ; Colour Sergeant Barrett, 2nd Lancashire ; and Corporal Richardson, 2nd Cambridge. The tie was shot off imme- diately, and the result was that Jackson won the gold medal, Barrett coming second and Richardson third. Before making their final venture the three marksmen had aereed to divide equally the three first nioney prizes, in all £350. Jackson, it should b- noted, tied with Captain Cortis on Saturday in the shooting for the silver medal, and was beaten by that officer in firing off the tie. In the match Australians v. Liverpool and District, on Saturday, whatever chance the Liverpool and District eleven had of defeating the Australians was spoiled by the rain. Perhaps the surprise of the match was the excellent display with the bat made by Shore, who held his position in the local team for bowling. His 42 (not out) and Mr. E. C. Horoby's 46 materially assisted Mr. Allan Steels's efforts in placing the Liverpool score 52 in advance of the Colonials on the first innings. The visitors, in their second venture, had to sacrifice four wickets to Tab off the arrears owing. The Australian captain compiled his 80 with much style and finish. At the stage in which the match was aban- doned the local eleven had much the best of the game, as the Australians were only 89 runs on with but two wickets t.) fall.

There was some curious cricket at Brighton, on Wednes- day. in the finish of the match between Sussex and Surrey, who at one time looked like winning very easily, only ob- taining a three wickets victory at the finish, thanks to some plucky batting by Mr. Newham and (Waite. The Sussex innings defied for 207, which left the visitors 92 to get to win; 50 went np with but one batsman out, and then the others fell chiefly through a lot of rash hitting. The game was continued during the usual lunch.on time in order to finieh. and in the end Rowley made the winning stroke at 25 minutes past two. At Lord's, on W,dneeday, the Australians did not make anything of a fight against the England team, and at a qua, ter-past three the match was all over, Eogland gaining an easy victory by an innings and 106 runs. The Austra- lians had lost one wicaet for twelve runs in their second innings, and were still 220 behind. With the game in such a position the Australians could not hope to win, but it was generally thought they would make a big effort to save the game. Up to a certain point they did very well, 90 being on the board with two wickets down. At 91, however, Jones was bowled, and his downfall proved to be the turning point of the game, for after hie dismissal the remaining seven winkets actually fell for 35 runs. The Englisk bowl- ing was very good, and the honours again rested with Briggs, who obtained six wicketa for 45 runs. In the whole match the Lancashire professional took eleven wickets for 74 runs, and thus completely silenced the objections that had been taken to his inclusien in the eleven. He bowted wonderfully well in both innings. _ . _ _ .

In dull weather Cheshire and Yorkshire concluded their match at Hull on Saturday, 'Yorkshire winning by two wickets, after an exciting finish. Cheshire's second inn- ings closed for 134, Crosfield taking his bat right through the innings for 52. Yorkshire had only 111 to get to win, but they started very badly, losing eight wickets for 79, and it was only the steady play of Emmott and Lee that eaabled them to win.

Self-control consists in the wilful and intentional clos- ing of the mind against dubious views and the heart against passions. A lady lecturer believes that women ought to retain their own names when they get married. She, has re- tained hers thus far. SUDDEN DEATH IN TIM EXEIIBITION. Abitit seven o'clock on Monday evening, while an elderly widow lady, from the neighbourhood of Stockport, was walking through the Italian section of the Liverpool Exhibition, accompanied by her daughter and son-in-law, she fell down in a swoon. She was at once carried into the open air, and Dr. Beattie, the Exhibition surgeon, was sent for. Although she ap- peartd to revive somewhat she never rallied, and died, not- withstanding medical care, within half an hour after her seizure, to the unconsolable grierof her relatives. The body was removed to the mortuary close at hand. Death is supposed to have been due to heart disease.

A NOT HER CHOIR SCANDAL. Sir,—l find the churchgoers of Haydock do not agree with the manner in which the organist and choirmaster of St. James' Church fulfils his duties. It appears that not long ago he invited three persons to join the choir simply because they were his playmates. He knew very well that all the choir seats were occupied, but notwithstanding this he insisted upon having their names on the list, the conse- quence being that last Sunday evening the church was the sr,•ene of a slight disturbance. One young man belonging to the choir quitted the church owing to having nowhere to sit durilig the service, one of the three persons taking his place. Now I and a great many others do not think this at all right, b,ca use the young man named has teen in the choir for upwards of six years. Now, if the organist would not exerciF.e so much authority in doing as he liked, the church would. once again be as it was some few years ago, and not in the position it is at pres6nt ; it wc,ul4 thrive and be a blessing to the parish in which it is situated. The church is not erected for persons to go and witness such disturbances as these, but for people who wish to !raise God in something like a peaceful sort of a manner. Hoping the churchwardens and sidemen will take the matter in hand as soon as they pos- sibly can, I will wait patiently and see what the conclusion will be.—Yours &tr.,
CriURCLIMAN.
ALLEGED DRINKING AT WILDERSPOOL BREWERY:
UNFOUNDED STATEMENT.

Sir,—Heving seen in your issue cf Saturday last a report of a " Drunk an,i disorderly case," tried at the Borough Court, in which the defendants, Costello and Maanion, were asked by the magistrates where they got their beer from and who naid for it, I find they are reported to have said they were the men "that run up the flag " and helped to fire the cannons at Wilders- pool Brewery, and that they, at the brewery, received beer in bucketsful. Now, sir, there are at present extensive al- terations being made at the above brewery by Messrs H. Neill and Sons, Manchester. lam in chareee of the same, and in common fairness I most emphatically deny both the pri- soners' statements, for they are utterly false and without the slightest found ,tioa ; in fact, Costello is working for us, and was at the time of the electioa, but Mannion never did. neither is be known to me or the firm I represent. It is an absolute falsehood for them to say " they run up the flae,-" or " helped to fire the cmnons." They had nothing to do with them whatever, neither had they "eeer in buckets- ful," for there was no beer whatever given to the men on this particular °cc ision, nor has there over been, as it is strictly forbidden. Trusting you will in fairness give the above sdace in your next issue.—l remain, yours truly. July 21, 1883. JOHN ASHLEY. [Our corresnonlent will see that we have referred to this matter tinder the bead of "Touch and Go," and that we agree with him as to the statements of Costello and Maznion beieLe groundless.—En. Er.]

div.head: SUTTON CHURCH DIFFERENCES.
div.p: THE SUTTON CHURCH DIFFERENCES.

Sir,—For SOMJ time reports of Sutton oburch and parish appeared weekly in one of our local papers. It is the general opinion that those ridiculoua and laughable puffs were written by one who interfered too much in parochial aff tirs, and has made hirnielf offensive to many. The abrupt ,•top to those reports at a particular time confirms this opinion. Better had be not put pen to paper, if the same who pub- lished inaccurate statements last October about our bishop and the Vicar of .!14utton, as to the cause of the vicar's notice to his curate. The insinuations on the vicar and bishop would have led the public to believe his lordship had for- gotten his pos'tion as bishop, and politeness as gentleman. His lordship showed kind, considerate, and prompt attention to all the vicar's wishes, immediately sending a gentleman to arrange -Arta, as curate-in-charge, at the same time directing his carate to give his vicar shorter notice. This action contradicted one audacious and false report. Another "by his lordship's permission," I should like plumply to contradict. When the present curate was appointed, the vicar did not rehract, his voluntary offer of £2OO stipend to a gentleman and good curate-in-charge for a certain time. Therefore I will thank the reporter to insure to hire the large income he so incorrectly, boldly, and confidently pub- lished the vicar receives: also if he will point out, "what others cannot see," the wonderful improvements in his parish by his curate. Thiess reports have detracted much from the curate's credit and position. The vicar or his friends may next cell for proofs as to all untruths so pub- lically circulated.—Yours. &c.. AN ADVOCATE FOR TRUTH.

div.head: REPORTED OUHAGE IN HALL-STREET.
div.p: REPORTED OUHAGE IN HALL-STREET.

Sir,—l was much surprised to read in your paper of S it- tirdav, July 10th, an account of an outrage said to have been committed in Hill-strest on the night of the election. I intended writing to you last weelt, but I thougbt someong more able than myself would have done so. I have lived in the neighbourhood for six years, and knowing the majority of the people I was astonished to read such an account ; consequently I made inquiries which lead mu to believe that the account of what took place is a gross misrepras..ntatiou of facts, and contains nothing but a tissue of falsehoods. Firstly, the horse was not maltreated. Secondly, the gate was not maliciously thrown drown and broker. Thirdly, the stabla was not pulled down. Fourthly. as far as I can learn, no•eggs were broken; and, as for the do!r, lam informed it was not hurt. Now, sir, if your report of the affair be true, three police constables were on the scene, and, as far as I can make out, they had no damage pointed out to them. If that had been done, the offenders could easily have been brought to justice, as all the p irties who were in the street at the time alleged live close to and are well known. I should not have troubled yen with this letter, only I think it is but fair to the inhabitants of Hall-street, and for the credit of your paper that the facts should be made known. lamat a lose to understand where your correspon- dent got his information from, but I do not believe you would knowingly allow such a report to appear in your paper unless it were true. I must apologies for troubling you, and hope you will find room for this in your next.—Belieys me, yours, STEPHEN JOHNSON.

15, Academy-street, Warrington. lit does rot appear from our correspondent's letter that he carefully read the report he takes exceptien to. It was not stated that the people of Hall-street were the perpetra- tors of the violence, but simply that the violence was per- petrated in Hall-street by a mob that" evidently con- tained a good deal of the roughest element of the town." According to our report the gate vras not "maliciously " broken, nor was the " stable " "pulled down." Toe in- quiries of our correspondent have 2vidently been made in an unreliable quarter, for the entire accuracy of our report is anirmed by those who are likely to best know the cir- cumstances of the disturbance. He is als ), we believe, en- tirely wrong in saying that three constables were present to whom the damage might have been pointed out.— ED. E.:;•.1

div.head: WIDNES DIVISION ELECTION.
div.p: WIDNES DIVISION ELECTION.

Sir,—We 'nave again been defeated in our division of the county, and I think it will not be uoinstructive to try and discover the cause. Mr. ',Moss's majority has been reduced more than one-half, and our numbers raised from 2.650 to '2,0:27.0r almost 300 more than at the last election. Not- withstanding abstentions we make a better show than we did last year. So far this is satisfactory, and had nor weak- kneed brethren not deserted us, but voted with us, we should have won. Had they remained neutral, we should have been almost equal. It requires more than common patience to speak of these brethren, and my hope is that they will be taught a lesson by the Conservatives not easily forgotten. Horne Rule must and will be given whichever party is in office. Should the Conservatives succeed to power, they will swallow all they have said against it, as they did in the case of the extension of the franchise, and will bring in a bill as Mr. Disraeli did going even further than Mr. Glad- stone, and our "Liberal" friends will be "sold." I sincerely hope it may be 20. But the principal cause of our defeat is to be traced to the apathy at headquarters. 1. Our candidate was late in coming into the field. 2. The district was not properly polled or canvassed. 3. A great deal was sacrificed to economy. Now, I would suggest that the candidate to con- test the division at the next election be selected at once, and as Mr. Birrell has shown himself everything we can possibly desire, that he be approached immediately and his promise obtained. We could return him without expense to himself. 4th. The books should be re-issned to the workers who called upon the electcrs, and those who have no paricniar colour should be pledged. Workers will ap- preciate the force and meaning of this. I know of many voters who would have voted for Birrell bad they been soli- cited to do so early, but everything was so hurried that system was conspicuous by its absence. Then as to economy. It appeared to all of us that cheese- paring was the order of the day—you will understand I am speaking of the Huyton and Roby district—And valuable time that should have been utilised in other directions was frittered away in extracting attention to our wants at headquarters.' The Hayton district should have a sub- agent appointed nnder Mr. Shores. It is folly having to conimunicate with Widnes every time a difficulty or a want Crone up. Then again I would suggest, if it can be done, that a nollin4 station be ()panel at Whiston. Why should some hundreds of voters be brought two or three miles to record their vstes when they can perform that duty close to their own hono.s I feel convinced this would be done if the Tories lead a maiority at Whiston. One polling station is too I:ttle for so large a district. There a-e other points that will readily suzgest them- selves, such as eallintr, meetings of the Liberals to bear lec- tures, receiving reports, dm, but what I particularly wish to ensphasiee is, haviog our work well in hand, and not being called upon to compress six months work into a fortnight Our c:rairman derrves every credit for the way he worked, and too great praise cannot be awarded him. But he had all kind of disadvantages to contend against—disadvantages s which should never have been allowed to exist, and I hope, in concluaion, that we snail insist at our next meeting of the diorict committee that some remedy be found for them. I commend those Fuggestiops to the pewers that be. If no attention is paid to them it will be evident that no real desire to win exists.—l am, sir, yours truly. Roby. J. HAWKINS.

POLITICS VERSUS LABOUR. Sir,—The elections are now over, working-men may now sit down and calmly reckon up the results. How many there nlgily be who could express satisfaction I cannot say, but I may venture to assert that not two representative working- men could be found in the kingdom but what would declare that the new electorate bad lost their heads.

A United Kingdom (?) has been called upon, by plebiscite. to give its opinion upon Home Rule. The answer given should startle the dis-anionists ; Scotland and Wales sympa- thize with Ireland; England by its vote declares in favour of its own arrogant supremacy, declares in favour of a cen- tralistation that must inevitably bring about such a state of congestion that leads me to think we :shall all before long be willing to perform the happy despatch. A few short months ago we were priding ourselves on having snit to the House of Commons men who, knowing, workmen's wants, would be able to press those wants to the front. It has been said that Englishmen, above all things, respect the laws and wish to bring about the necessary changes in a lawful and peaceable manner, and yet what have w, seen during the past fortnight? Why, the very means that wiser heads than ours have fought for since 1832 thrown away and despised. It may be that workmen do not fully realise the issue at stake, that, carried away with shouts about Empire, they fail to see that the "classes" are only anxious to create, and keep, happy hunting grounds wherein the scores of so-called "noble hot.ses " may find occupation at the workers' expense. It this be so lam afraid they are destined to have a rude awakening. A small Blue-book has just been issued giving particulars of the recent disturbances in France and Belgium. To those who are satisfie i with things as they are the recalling of this mast be somewhat disquieting; to workmen it should come as a revelation of the future. Belgium, a small state,

is now given up almost entirely to the manufacture of iron, and small though it may be, it seems to affect the iron mar- kets of the world ; and yet we read that "The Belgian coal industry is on the verge of ruin under the pressure of corn- petition from Russia and France. For nine years the profit on capital has not exceeded 11 per cent." rn their anxiety to get orders, Belgian girder manufacturers actually offer English architects and engineers 2 per cent on all orders sent to them. Throughout the whole of the miming dis- tricts the average wage earned is 2fr. 71c., or put it, that all that heads of families can earn is about 2s 61 per day. Worse than all this, thousands of husbands, wives, sells, and daughters, work together in the pite, with the poor satisfac- tion of knowing that the truck system, and wages paid monthly, will deprive them even of the paltry 2a 61 per day. The Belgian miner who earned in 1873 71r. 80c. now earns 2tr. 99c. We talk of reductions in England, hut this is something awful to contemplate But what of the French miners who are competing with those of Belgium ? At Like. where the miners have been out on striks, it is im- possible to realise the misery in which the population of 30,000 are steeped. A report states : "It would be impos- sible to reduce wages further, ne matter for what grade of workers, for*they have already reached the extreme limit." The most .skilful workers make about 13 aSd in a day of twelve hours; the men are discouraged and "they go to work listlessly and whhout hope." Lord Vivian, our representative, reporting this deplorable state of things from Brussels, and referrlng to the recent riots, says If the miners were better informed as to the condition of the Belgian coal industry. they would see the unreasonableness of their demand.' Well, this may be so, but I have an impression that were Lord Vivian earning even his present salary under conditions im which the miners of Decaz wine earn theirs he would throw sweet resonablenees to the winds. In some of the pits " there are regions of sub- terranean fire that cannot ha approached, and fl.:mes play about their summits in the darkness of the night. Train rails are laid along the permanent waye, and the trucks are driven by horse or steam power in lines liquid with slush." I have said that this report oaeht to appear as a revelation to wotkingmien. I happen, unfortunately, to be one who ' thinks that a chain cannot possibly be stronger than the weakest link will allow. Looking upon la.lesur as one huge chain, that encircles the detestable word, competition, I am driven to the conclusion that either Competition must cease to have its present hateful form, or the weakest link, viz., the low price paid for labour on the Continent, will snap, and the present wage paid for English labour will, with a featful rush, go very much lower. I may be asked what politics has to do with this ? I answer a great deal. In the first place, I have noticed that Conservative papers pride themselves very much upon the fact that Prince Bismarck prefers Lord Salisbury as Premier to Mr. Gladstone, mad I ask why is this ?. Why should the min who•keeps such a tight grip on this throat of the German labeursr look with favour upon one, more than another, of our English statesmen? Workmen open your eyes and you will see the,: the land that, through its Liberalism, oecned wide its arms to a Mazzini, a Garibaldi, a Ko:suth, and a host of releil patriots is not likely to be the tool of this man sf blood and iron, unless it is ruled by a Tory Patrician whose sympathies are with his class. Why is Mr. Glads'one disliked by the statesmen of other countries? The answer should be clear to all who have studied the history of the past twentv-five years. He has sympathized with struggling nationalities, and striven at I all times to give to his own peop'e the responsibility of power. For this he is hated by the " classes "at home and by rulers abroad he is detested. The more liberty English- men get the less possible is it for German, Austrian, or Rus- sian Emperors to grind their plonle; and the less the foreign workman is tinder the heel of a despotic soldiery, the less keen will he feel the poisoned tooth of competition. The moral of my Calf, is—working-men ciiee to support men who are held back by an antiquated reverence for the past. and support only those who, having studied labour qusetiene, know the labourers' wants. July, 1886. HENRY WH(THAM.

EXTRAORDINARY THEFT OF A HORSE.

Abraham Kenworthy (27), who was described as a sand hawker and horse dealer, of Oldham, was brought before Mr. C. Broadbent, at the War- rington Borough Police Court, on Tuesday morning, on a charge of stealing a bay mare, valued at £24. the property of John Glover, on the previous day. From a statement made by Chief Constable Hunt, it appeared that on Monday afternoon, when the horse fair was being held in Winwick-street, John Glover, Richard Glover, and their sister, farmers at Rainford, near St. Helens, were at the fair bargain- iifg with two or three men, not in custody, about the price of a mare. At the time prisoner and four other men were there, and prosecutor had a horse which he valued at £24, and for which he wanted £l9 10s, and another horse. The party then went into the Old Ball public-house to try and strike a bargain, and Richard Glover remained at the door holding the horse. John Glover, his sister, the pri- soner, and another man remained a time in the house, when a dispute arose as to the cash being paid down. Kenworthy then said " Never mind the money; I have plenty and am paymaster of this lot." One of the men then went outside and told Richard Glover, who was still holding the horse, that the bargain was made and the money paid. Rd. Glover desired to see his brother before giving up possession of the animal, and the man then struck Richard Glover, snatched the animal from him, jumped on its back, and galloped away las hard as he could. Richard Glosrer told those in the house what had oecurred, whereupon prisoner and the other men rushed out of the house, got into ' a cart, and drove rapidly in the direction of the Horse and Jockey. Information was given to the 1, police, and P.C.'s Neill and Glover went on Man- chester-road, and at the Rope and Anchor it was ' ascertained that four men had driven past, one ' horse being in the shafts, and the other fastened behind. Prisoner was apprehended soon afterwards at the Dog and Partridge, where he was having his tea, and he then said that. when he found that the horse had been come by dishonestly he got out of the trap and would have nothing to do with it. Pri- soner was then remanded. Mr. A Browne, who ap- peared on his behalf, asked for bail. Prisoner, who, he said, had over £6O in his possession, had given all the information that he could to the police. Chief .Constable Hunt opposed the application, which was not granted. At the Borough Court, yesterday morning, pri- soner Kenworthy was brought up on remand, and a man named Isaac Smith, also a horse dealer, of Lees, near Oldham, was put f6rward with him on the same charge. Mr. A. Browne appeared on be- half of the prisoners. Chief Constable Hunt again stated the particulars of the case, and said that he was led to believe that Smith was the man who jumped on the horse that was alleged to have been stolen. The horse had since been recovered at Lees, near Oldham, in the possession of Smith, and had been brought to Warrington. Mr, Hunt asked for a remand. Mr. Browne asked that some evidence for the prosecution be taken, which was done.— John Glover said that on the day in question he held the mare at the door of the public-house. Pri- soner Smith was the man who came out of the house and, saying that the horse was bought, knocked him down, jumped on its back, and gal- loped away. Kenworthy was the man who said he had the money and would pay for the mare.—Mr. Browne intimated that the defence would be that the horse was bought. He did not oppose the applica- tion for a remand, but asked that the case should be fixed either for Wednesday or before that day. He had, he mentioned, engaged counsel for the de- fence. Mr. Hunt wished a remand until next Friday, as the police wanted to secure other men concerned. Mr. Browne said he had a complee answer to the case. The Bench remanded prisoners until Wednesday, it being understood that they would again be remanded if the case was not then complete. Mr. Browne then applied for bail, say- ing that he could offer bail to the amount of thou- sands of pounds at that moment. Mr. Hunt opposed the application, which was not granted.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 24, 188 g.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 24, 188 g.
THE NORTIIWICH ELECTION. HOW THE BATTLE WAS FOUGHT.

Seconding a resolution of thanka to Mr. Brett at a Liberal meeting at North wich on Monday eveninir. Mr. A. Fletcher, the Liberal agent, said they had had very few Unionists in Northwich—(hear, hear)—but a lot of tradesmen. Trade and politics were different things, but, unfortunately, trade in that district had overcome politics. They stood on that platform with easy consciences. He would rather have defeat under the conditions under which they had experi- enced it than victory by the loss of principle. They hadn't whatever they had done, debauched the con- stituency. (Cheers.) On the day after the last elec- tion—whatever might be said about the Ho-called riot which took place on the day of election—there was no- thing like the drunkenness that there had been this last week No one could say that Mr. Brunner or his committee resor- ted to tricks to catch votes. ("No.'i No one could say *hat in getting their nomination papers filled up they tried to mislead the puplic by putting the names of well-known Liberals down when they were the names of obscure indi- viduals. They did not go to a labourer at Wharton whose name happened to be like that of the leading Liberal, and ask him to sign a nomination paper in order that the poor people might be misled. They had had great odds ;4gainst them, for the simple reason that the Tory organisation, with all its Primrose leaguery and buffoonery, was placed at the disposal of Mr. Robert Verdin and those who worked with him. He had experienced one of the keenest disappoint- ments of his life in the defeat of Mr. Brunner, and assured them he wondered where the cause of the disaster was. If it was any fault on the part of the organisation he was afraid he must share in it. but he had fought it as he thought a political battle should be fought. (Cheers.) Misrepresentations had been spread abroad since the result was declared. He had been told seriously by a man who ought to have known better that men had been dismissed from Winnington because of the way in which they had voted. He gave the most unqualified contradiction to that statement. (Cheers.) He believed the way in which Mr. Brunner had taken his defeat had made them more fond of him than ever they were before. (Cheers.) His name was associated with the true Liberals of the constituency. (Cheers.)

div.head: MR. BRUNNER ON HIS PA.RLIA.ME NTA.RY CAREER
div.p: MR. BRUNNER ON HIS PA.RLIA.ME NTA.RY CAREER
A PROGRAMME OF REFORM.

Mr. J. T. Brunner, speaking in response to a resolution of thanks to himself for his services to Liberalism in Cheshire at a meeting at Northwich, on Monday night, thanked his supporters for their service. He believed, he said, that the soreness produced by the work of April last year hid lasted until now, and that a large number of men had not voted against him and for Mr. Verdin for political reasons at all. (Hear, hear.) Pressure had been put upon men to vote against their will, against their wish. (Hear, hear.) There had been prominent men—men who had been known to be brought up in Liberal principles, who were strong for the Bill, strong for Home Rule, strong for justice to Ire- land, warm •supporters of Mr. Gladstone six weeks ago, who had been working very hard against Home Rule and for the Uaion since. (" Shame.") After alluding to the other Liberal candidates in Cheshire who had failed, Mr. Brunner said Mr. Gladstone had failed for the day, but he would carry the banner of Christian love and charity to Ireland aloft until it wins a glorious victory. (Cheers.) The Parliament now elected was abso- lutely impotent for good. It was one in which no side bad a majority. He did not believe that it was on account of his vote for the bill for the better government of Ireland that ha was opposed by the Tories. His record in the last Parliament was too good a one to please the Tories. (Laughter and cheers.) He had promised that he would vote for allotments for labouring. men In country districts, that he woeld always help oppressed people, and esmcially people who were op- pressed by landlords. (Hear. hear.) He voted steadily with the representatives of the crofters. (Hear, hear') -Away in the far north of Scotland there were thousands of men who, like the peasants of Irel and, were the descendants of the rightful owners of the soil—(hear, hear)—men who had been, through the provision of parchment law intro- duced from England, deprived of their just rights like the Irishmen, and Mr. Gladstone's Government made an effort which nearly every etedicel in the House thought was a feeble effort to mend the condition of these men. He (Mr. Brunner) endeavoured to strengthen the provisions of that bill for the benefit of tbe crofters. He voted for temperance reform—(cheers)—and since lest Wednesday he had thanked God he voted for temperance principles (Cheers.) He voted for the radical reform of the House of Lords. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) He did not think they would get much good until there was a radical reform of the House of Lords. (Cneers.) He voted fer tee reform of local government—(hear, hear,)—and for the re- form of local government in Ireland, too, and again, like many a man before him, with no i-ff.mt, for the Lords had determined that no anaendment should be made in the matter of local government in Ireland. Lastly. he voted—and be was very proud of it, and thankful that he had the op- portunity of voting—for religious equality in Scotland and Waliss—(ehoers)—end he trusted some day to have the opportunity of voting in favour of ab- solute religious equality for England. (Cheers ) He He had a request a while ago to give £l,OOO to, church. (Laughter.) His correspondent was very modest, and not pressing, because he gave a little latitude; he would not absolutely fix the figure at £l,OOO he (Mr. Brunner) might go to £1,450, which was half the debt, if he liked. (Laughter.) In the matter of subscriptions he had always been for religious equality. (Hear, hear, and a : " May you live long for it.") Every measure such as he bad enumerated—fofr allotments, for land reform, for the reform of the House of Lords, for temperance reform, for the reform of local government, for religious eauelity—he was ready to work for outside Parliament as inside Par- liament—(cheers)—and it might be that considering what sort of a Parliament hid been elected, he should be able to do more to help these questions forward living in Winnington than living at Palace Chambers. (Cheers.) They wanted a very thorough reform .of the land laws in the three kingdoms. (Hear, hear.) They wanted a reform of the land laws in Ireland, but Liberals would be thoroughly satisfied to lot Irishmen reform them: (Cheers.) Now, when they got Home Rule for England, they wished for a thoroughly Radical measure of reform of the land laws. They also wanted agricultural tenancies amended. They wanted mining royalties rated:and taxed—(eheers)— and in a good many instances, they wanted them largely reduced, for when wages were coming down it was very hard to find a man who did nothing and never had done anything in the way of work, for himself or anyone else, getting day by day and year by year tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands of pounds, whilst men's comforts were lessened, men's children lees well fed and lees well clothed They wanted free elementary education, and more. They wart the children in this country far better taught than they had been. (Hear. bear.) In this matter of eeucetion they should agree together so as to spend their money as to produce the best possible results. He wanted it to be brought about that no longer should men lee so far untaught that they were fit for nothing but common labour. He did not believe for a moment that common labour would be one whit the less well done if every man was taught a trade, and had it right at his finger ends. (Cheers.) If they did not make up their minds to have their children taught as well as children are taught in other parts of the world, depend upon it that they worde go down in- stead of going forward in this life. (Cheers.) He wanted, both with regard to local and Parliamentary affairs, one man to have one vote. One man was as good as another—(hear, bear)—and a man at a salt pan, from the point of view of the general body of society, was as good as a man on the cushions of a large carriage. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) They had no Liberal representative for the Northwich Division If they wanted any Liberal work done in Parliament for the Northwich Division, Mr. Ellis bad kindly undertaken to do it. (Loud cheers.) He would be found at the old address, No. 132, Palace Chambers, Bridge-street, Westminieter, within two minutes' walk of the House of Commons. They were going to have another fight, and what were they to do in the meantime to prepare for it? He said, hold themselves together. Not only should they meet together for werk, hut for play, and in their amusements. He coun- selled them to get toeether, gat together often, and enjoy themselves well together. To hold themselves together, net only for their own sakes, but for the sake of their country, for the sake of their children, and for the sake of their chil- dren's children. (Laud cheers.)

GOOD Tr3EPIARY. --The weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Tempters was held in the lodge-room, Bridge-street. on Monday evening, tinder the presidency of Brother J. Macdonald. W.C.T. There was a very rod attendance of members. After one new member had been initiated arrangements were completed for the lodge to take part in forthcoming united temperance demonstrations at Ashton. Newton, and the Liverpool Exhi- bition. The evening's programme was "Mal Bag Night," and a number of interesting communieltioos were read from Brother W. H. Richardson, W.D., secretary of South Shields, Durham; Brother J. West, L.D., of Chowlaent ; and others, and an amusing communication was also read, signed " Cleopatra's 'Needle." The session throughout was a very enjoyable one. WINDOW GLASS WORKERS' UNITEBSAL FEDER&T/ON. —The third annual congress of the Window Glass Workers' Universal Federation concluded its labours on Saturday last, after a session extmding from the previous Tuesday. The session was held in the Assembly Room, Settee Arms. St Helens. and the following representatives were present : —Mr. James Campbell, of Pittsburgh, Pa , president ; Mr. John Gerrard, of Plank-lane, Lancashire, vice-president ; Mr. Albert Delwarte, of Charleroi, Belgium, secretary, and the following delezates :—Messrs. Samuel A. Wallace and John H. Winters, America; John G. Schlicker, Jos. French, and James B7own, Sunderland ; Joseph Norbury.St. Helens; E France; Ernest Stenger and Louis Jacquet, Belgium; Lm-,1"Ca;lo Grismeyer and Peggio Merteto, Italy. The Proceedings were private. The first °lngress was held in St. Helens, in June 1531, after a preparative congress held at Charleroi, the second at Pittsburg, Pa., on July 14th and followin, days, 1585. It will thus be seen that St. Helens has already been honoured with two of the first conventions since the formation of the association in 1884. From what can be seen, the bond of unity existing between the various national branches of the countries embraced by the Federa- tion, is being firmly ?onsolidated. Immediately after the termination of the session the delegates left the town ix a body.

NEWTON.

The Liverpool employ6s of the London and North-Western Railway Company held their twenty-second annual picnic and athletic festival at the Castle-hill Field, Newton, which bad been kindly placed at their disposal by Colonel Mc- Corquodale. A more delightful or suitable spot could scarcely have been chosen, and, as far as the unpropitious character of the weather permitted, an extremely pleasant day was spent by the excursionists. The principal events of the afternoon were the athletic sports, which had been so arranged as to give all the employes, old and young, an bpportunity of entering the list 4„ and the utmost good humour prevailed throughout the competitions. The offi- eials were Mr H B Taylor (chairman), Mr Frank Rea (judge), Mr. H. Metcalf (referee), Mr Crailte and Mr J Bir- me (clerks of the course), Mr Fowler and Mr MeFie (starters), Mr E Eastwood (handicapper), Mr Gillies (treas- urer). and Mr T Williams (hon. secretary), in addition to whom there was a staff of active stewards. Reaults of the sports :-220 yards flat race handicap (restricted to youths under 18) : 1 W G Harbour, 4 yards start; 2 S C Foulkes, 4 yards; 3, T Roberts, scratch. 220 yards flat race (open to the office staffs of all railway Lompanies and their agents in Liverpool : 1 J Burns (Lancashire and Yorkithire); 2 L Murphy (London and North-Western) ; 3 J Fairclough (Lancashire and Yorkshire). 120 yards flat race handicap: 1 A Al Haynes, 9 yards start; 2 T W Glelee, 9 yards; 3 F E Roberts, 3 yards One mile walking handicap (confined to youths under 18) : 1 J H Currier, 25 yards start ; 2 W Roy, 20 yards; 38 C Foulkes, 30 yards. 220 yards hurdle race: 1 L Murphy, scratch; 2 T W Gleave, 10 yards start; 3, W Tomkinson. 14 yards. 220 yards flat race (far per- sons 35 years old and upwards) : 1 T Williams, 10 yards start; 2 J Williams, scratch ; 3 Mackenzie M‘Leod, 20 yards. Half-mile flat race: 1 F B Jackson, 10 yards start; 2 J Bain, 30 yards; 3 A M Maynes, scratch. 190 yards sack race (for youths under 18) : 1 J Boothbv, 6 yards start; 2 T Roberts, scratch. 440 yards flat race 1 L Murphy, scratch ; F E Roberts, 25 yards ; 3 J Shaw, 10 yards. Potato gathering contest: 1 T Lusby; 2 W Evans; 3 L Murphy. One mils flat race: 1 F B Jackson. 20 yards start; 2 J Bain, 90 yards; 3 F Dodd, 80 yards. 120 yards flat race (open only to married men of the committee): 1 T Williams, 7 yards start; 2 J Williams, scratch ; 3 J D Grundy, 1 yard. 220 yards consolation race (limited to compeiitors of the London and North-Western Railway Company who had not previously gained a prize) : 1 W H Allerton ; 2 Ellis; 3 C Dodd. In the absence of Mr David Taylor, the prizs were difeributed to the successful competitors by Mr Frank Bee. Subsequently the excursionists partook of an excellent repast. provided in a spacious tent by Mr J Walton, Victoria Hotel, Urmston. Selections of music were played diving the day by the band of the traffic department, Edgehill.

div.head: CRAWFoRD DIVoIICIE CASE.
div.p: THE CRAWFoRD DIVoIICIE CASE.

In anticipation of Friday being the last day of this remarkable trial, the entrances of the Divorce Court were besieged with people anxious to gain admission some time before the proceedings commenced. The officials, however, took every precaution to prevent overcrowding, anki many finding it impossible to get into the court went away, Sir James Hannen took his seat at half-past ten, the jury having previoualy entered their box. Sir Charles Mika occupied the same place at the solicitors' table as he had done throughout the bearing of the case, but Mrs. Craw- ford, although in the vicinity, was not in court. On the case being called on, Sir Walter Phillimore re- sumed his address to the court and jury on behalf of the case for the Queen's Procter. He reviewed the evidence at length with a view to showing that it was impossible- that Sir Charles Dilke could have been guilty of adultery under the circumstances stated. His final submission was that they would not have to decide whether Mr. Crawford was to have a divorce, but whether he was to have one on these conditions, Sir Charles Dilke being the co-respondent. Mr. Crawford would have no difficulty in obtaining a decree noon the evidence which had been, given both by Mrs. Crawford and Captain Forster. At the time the confession was made there was no doubt that Mrs. Crawford was a thoroughly degraded woman, had been to a brothel with Captaim Forster, and had committed various acts of adul- tery. What they would have to consider was whether she had been guilty of the double adultery, and whether she was right in saying that she fell a victim to Sir Charles Dilke, with whom she had told her husband she was not enamoured. It was, therefore, for tbem to consider, subject to his lordship's directions, whether she was an adultress with Sir Charles Dilke or not, and there he left the matter in their hands.

The Pre-el-dent then proceeded to stun up the case to the jury. He said that before commencing with the evidence he 'must remind them of the origin and nature of the pro- ceedings. Mr. Crawford accused his wife of adultery with Sir C. Dilke, and he established her adultery to the satisfac- tion of Mr. Justice Butt. He was entitled to have the decree of Mr. Justice Butt made adeolute unless it were established that the finding was centrary to justice. The evidence consisted mainly of confessions made by Mrs. Crawford. No one throughout impeached Mr, Crawford's honour or veracity. Mrs. Crawford was present in court on that occasion, represented by coutisel, who said no doubt it was part of her case that she was guilty. Sir Charles Dilke was also present at that trial. Remembering these facts after Mr. Crawford's evidence what other result could possibly follow than that the learned judge, acting on the confession of the wife and the evidence produced, made the decree which was now sought to be upset? The Queen's Proctor now said that Mrs. Crawford's confession was not a true confession, hut an invention on her part, and that the real facts were the contrary to what she had said. If that had been established the Queen's Proctor must succeed. They must judge of the case according to their lights, ex- perience, and knowledge of the affairs of the world. Mrs. Crawford had come- forward and sworn publicly that her confession to her husband was true. Sir Charles Dino, on the other hand, had sworn it was false. The jury must determine between them, and having seen them face to face judge which was telling the truth, and which was sneaking fals.ly. They must also draw their own conclu- sion of Sir Charles Dilke's conduct at the last trial in sitting silently while a decree was being made for a disso- lution of Mr. Crawford's marriage upon a confession which, if his statement were true, he knew was a tissne of falsehoods seriously reflecting on his moral character.

THE DECISION. The jury retired to consider their verdict at seven minutes to three o'clock, and were absent only savant-en, minutes. On their return, they stated that in their opinion the decree was not obtained at the last trial contrary to justice. The intervention of the Queen's Proctor was con- sequently dismissed with costd, and his Lordship. intimated that facilities would be given to have the decree made abso- lute at once. There were no expressions of feeling in court. Sir Charles, who did not seem surprised, at once left, while Mr. Crawford, who staved a few moments later, was received with slight applause outside the court. The scene was un- expectedly devoid of excitement. ADDRESS OF SIR CHARLFS DILKE TO HIS LATE CONsmuENTs. The Central News says Sir Charles Dilke,, on Friday issued the following address to the electors of Chelsea : Gentlemen,You are aware that the inttrvention of the Queen's Proctor in the case of Crawford versus Crawford, on the plea that' the said divorce was pronounced contrary to the justice of the case," has led to a verdict in which the finding of Mr. Justice Batt has been affirmed. This de- cision has been come to without my being allowed to ap- pear by counsel, or to address the fury, without my being allowed to cross-examine for myself, and also without my being supplied with particulars or being given in advance

the names of witnesses, all of which under an order of the Court, were freely supplied to the other side. The Queen's Proctor, who accepted some of my suggestions for cross- examination, and Sir Walter Phillimore, who maintained my position with conspicuous ability, appearing, however, not as my advocate, but as the representative of a public official, were also placed at a great disadvantage by having practically to disclose the defence before the evidence in support of the charge was given. I have always known how difficult the cause would be even if presented. as I had reason to suppose it would be; but the method of procedure ordered by the Courts intensified that difficulty. As far as public life goes, I have no option but to accept the verdict, while protesting once more against its justice. Icm only, gentlemen, assure you, as I have already often solemnly assured you, and with equal solemnity sworn in Court, that I erg innocent of the charges brought against me, and respectfully and gratefully bid you farewell.—l am, .gentlemen, yours faithfully,
CHARLES W. DUKE.
PAR R'S BANKING COMPANY.

An extraordinary general meeting of the share- holders of the above Company was held at the Bank, Winwick-street, Warrington, on Friday morning. Mr. J. C. Parr, chairman, presided, and the other directors present were Sir Gil- bert Green&ll, M.P., Sir T. Frost, Messrs, D. Gamble, P. Stubs, E. Greenall, IL Woodcock, A. Hewlett, Geo. McCorquodale, J, Thompson, A. Turner, H. Warren Meade-King, and Cecil F. Parr. The meeting was held for the purpose of sanctioning the declaration of an interim dividend to be payable on the 26th inst., and for conducting the ordinary business of the Company.—The General Manager (Mr. Dun) read the directors' report, which stated that the business of the Company had been satisfactory, and that they recommended that there should be de- clared at that meeting an interim dividend at the rate of 15 per cent. per annum free of income tax. After providing for the dividend there remained a , considerable balance which would be carried for- I ward to the next account.—The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoption of the report, said he was happy to be able to inform them that business continued to maintain its steady progress, that the profits for the past half-year were very satisfactory, and that after paying the interim dividend which they were called upon to declare, they had a good surplus to carry forward to the next account.—Mr. E. GREENALL seconded the proposal, and the report was unanimously adopted.—Mr. IlurciriNGs moved that an interim dividend of 15 per cent. as recommended by the directors be de- clared.—Mr. SHARPE seconded this proposal, which was also agreed to unanimously.—Mr. IL DAVIES, in moving a vote of thanks to the chairman, said they had all heard a favourable report. Judging of what he could see in his little way he was of opinion that affairs were improving a little. There seemed to be a little more stir in ~he way of purchasing, and so far as he was able to judge, from what had fallen under his own notice, he thought that before long they should have a de- cided improvement in trade. (Hear, hear.) .In conclusion, he said they were all glad to see Mr. Parr in his position as -chairman.—Dr. BEAMAN seconded the proposal, which was cordially agreed to.—The CHAIRMAN, in acknowledging the compli- ment, thanked the gentlemen who had taken the I trouble to come to their meeting. It was a pleasure to the Board, and a great pleasuie to him as chair- man, to feel that the shareholders took an interest in the management and progress of their business, and were willing by their presence from time to time to support and encourage those upon whom the responsibility of management devolved. —This , was all the business.

div.head: LAT EST NE W.
div.p: LAT EST NE W.

Mr. Ruskin passed a restless night, but does not appear to be any weaker. Two constables were drowned on Friday whilst bathing at Stroudhill, near Sligo. Mr. J. P. Knight, general manager of the Brighton Rail- way, died suddenly on Friday morning of apoplexy. A telegram, elated New York, Friday. says : Mr. William Hunter, the Assistant-Secretary of State, died on Thursday. _ _ _

The cricket match between Yorkshire and the Austra- lians was stooped by rain On Friday afternoon until to-day, the score standing at 145 for five wickets. The Metropolitan police notify that a number of forged Bank of England notes. principally fifty pounds denomina- tion, but also one hundred pounds have lately appeared. _ _ _

The Queen stearmd for Cowes on 7ridav in the Royal yacht to witness the naval review. The Empress Eugenie accompanied her. liain fell heavily during the review. GREAT FIRE IN LosooN.7-Early on Friday morning the four-storeyed premis9s of Mr. W. J. Ramsey, printer. Clerk• enwell-green, London, were destroyed by fire, and the ad- joining business places of the United Electric Wire Com- pany, L'.lr. M•Carthy, and others were greatly damaged. The metropolitan firemen promptly subdued the fire. The damage will amount to riveral thousand poneds. RESPITE OF A MunDERER.—On Friday morning, Major Preston, the governor of StrangewAys Gaol, received a communication from the Home Office to the effect that John Waite, who was on Saturday last condemned to death for the murder of his wife at Bacup, had been respited during her Majesty's pleasure. Waite, apparently under the influence of jealousy, had cut his wife's throat and smashed in her skull.

DEEPENING OF THE DEE.—The vast Work of deepeninrt the Dee'from Chester to the sea is rapidly proceeding. The channel for the ebb tide flow of the tide has been straightened, and is much deeper. The consequence is that steamers of heavy draught can come right up to Connak's Quay. The steamer Eleanor, for instance, which before was unable to enter the Dee, has just successfully dis- charged a cargo for the North Wales Paper Company at Connalfs Quay. THE WIAIELEDON MEETING. The first prize in the Olympic competition was won on Friday by Private Lowe, of the Queen's Westminster, who, in ten shots, at 600 yards, succeeded in making 46 points—within four of the highest possible, The first prize of £lO in the " Graphic" series, shot for at 200 yards, any positi,.n, was won by Lance• Corporal Pollard, Ist Hants, with 35, the highest possible. Mr. Turner, of Birmingham, won the first prize of £25 in the Bass competition.

NIANSLATTGHTER CASE.—At Derby Assizs on Friday, Frederick Banting was indicted before Mr. Justice Stephen for the manslaughter, ;At Matlock, of a man named Reader. The facts were somewhat singular. The parties quarrelled on the way horns, and the prisoner struck the deceased in the throat. The latter sta:zgered a short distance and then died. It transpired that a branch of the deceased's jugular vein had been ruptured, and the surgeon who was sum- moned had not known a similar case. The prisoner was sentenced to ni-no months' imprisonment.

RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT PORTSMOUTIL—At Portsmouth, on Friday, a dockyard train with two hundred Colonists on it, passed the Admiral-Superintendent's office and swerved at the corner with great shock. The forepirt of the train took the right metals, but the shock shifted the points and the rear of the train took the wrong line. The rapidity with which the train was moving completely overturned one carrioge and two others went off the line. Six or seven persons were injured, including Chief Justice Pobson. None were seriously hurt. The Colonists were going to attend the Naval review.

div.head: SHIP CANAL SCHEME.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL SCHEME.

The "Times," on Friday, in its City article, referring to the Ship Canal scheme, says :—There is every reason to ' believe that the Manchester Ship Canal Cnnpany have failed to obttin that response from the public which they had anticipet ed. On Thursday afternoon rumour went so far as to say that the issue had been withdrawn, but that step has not as yet been taken, we believe. If the towns in- terested in the scheme really have as much confidence in it as is alleged, we do'not understand why they have not made the issue a success by their own unaided efforts. Unless the whole thine, is a big mistake, which we are loth to be- lieve, surely they could by a I,ttle energy have raised the greater pert of the money required without asking for sub- scriptions from the public. If that was impossible. it has been suezested tbat Manchester, Salford, and Warrington, which are more itnrnediately interested in the undertaking, might have obtained from Parliament power to levy a muni- cipal rate in order to provide soene minimum rate of interest, say 3 per cent., on the capital necessary to construct the canal. The exteet to which these centres of industry be- lieve in the euccese of tl•le undertaking may be roughly measured by the fact of their having sunk £146,000 in pre- liminary expenses, which will have been wasted if the canal is not made. We think it morally certain that it will even- tually be made, bat the half-hearted way in which the scheme has been supported by those most interested in it fully explains the disposition of the.general public to wait and see more clearly what its prospects are before asking for shares. The open enemies of the scheme are saying that no investor is it all anxious to put money into another " Hull and Barnsley "fiasco, and this spiteful observa- tion should serve ae a warning .to those concerned that they must put in "a little more powder" if they wish to succeed.' THE POLITICAL SITUATION.—LORD SALISBURY'S RETURN. The Marquis of Saliebury, accompanied by the Mar- chionese and Lord and Lady Cecil, arrived on Friday at Charing Croee Station by the 5-40 continental express train. The noble Marquis looked remarkably well after his jour- ney. He was met on arrival by his eldest son, Lord Cran- bourne, and by Sir Edward War kin, M.P., and the Chairman of the South-Eastern Railway. Only a few persons were admitted on the platform, but there were large crowds out- side the barriers and the approaches to the station, who loudly cheered his lordship as he drove to his residence in Arlington-street. The Press Association learns that the Marquis of Salisbury is desirous of conferring with his po:itical colleagues before visiting her Majesty. He has therefore arranged to spend Friday night in London. when an informal gathering of such of the members of the late Conservative Cabinet as are now in town will probab lv be held at Arlington-street, and his lordship will proceedto Osborne to-day (Saturday). The leading members of the Conservative party, most of whom have been taking advantage of the interval of quiet since the elections to obtain a little rest, are hurrying back to the mf-tropolis. The Carlton, Junior Carlton, and other Conservative clubs are already centres of activity, the at- tendance at the former having been greater on Thursday than for many months. Despite reports to the contrary, it is regarded as certain by responsible Conservatives that the new Cabinet will not include a Liberal Unionist. In the conversations at the Carlton respecting the distribution of portfolios in the new Administration, a strong feeling found expression in regard to the desirability of introducing fresh blood to the front bench. In this connection it is regarded as not improbable that at least three ex-Ministers may be elevated to the House of Lords. Mr. Gladstone, who is spending much time with his private sec,etaries just now in reference to official business, will remain at Downing-street until the visit of the out- going Ministry to Osborne. It is believed he will go to Hawarden immediately afterwards and remain there until Hence Hee meets in October, after the holidays. It is under- stood that the actual change of seals will not take place until Saturdly week, and that Lord Salisbury's 'Government will take over office on the following Monday. -Lord Hartingtora telegraphing to Mr. Howe, the Unionist candidate for Orkney atei Shetland, says:—"l am in favour of local %government for the three kingdom', not necessarily identical, but based on a similar principle."
SUSPECTED PLOT AGAINST PRESIDENT CLETE- LAND.

WASHINGTON, FRlDA.Y.—Pre3ident Cleveland returned here to-day from the Albany, where he had been attending the bicentennial celebration of the settlement. While the President was at the Albany he was persistently followed about by a man whose behaviour at length caused him to be arrested and imprisoned. On being examined, the man declared that his only object in following the President was to petition him for al4 office in the Government.

A now low-water landing pier at Ramsay, in the Isle of Man, 72.0 vv-ds in length, was opened on Thursday. Pro- vision is made for a tramway line to run from end to end of the pier. A SIGN OF TrtE TIMES —A scene was witnessed at Kildy- sari-, in County Cork, a few days ago which many English people may halm thought an impossibility. A National League meeting was addressed by an Irish World reporter, who lauded O'Donovan Roses and denounced Mr. Glad- stone. The uninformed American was forthwith dragged from the platform and "beaten severely," and, according, to a sub-inspector of constabulary, he would have been killed but for the timely arrival of the police. One of his assailants was brought befsre the magistrates on Wednesday, but he was only fined a nominal sum, the Bench, like the meeting, cons'clering t',at the complainant's speech vta,a fat a very aggravating character.

I THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. ° POULTRY HOUSES (Continued). In this country it is the custom to merely give as , much light as will pass through a small sky-light, or a window let into the wall on one side. In either case the window does not exceed a foot or 18 inches square, and it is very often the case that it is about a foot by six inches. This is, we think, a great mistake, and the American plan of giving a considerably greater amount of glass is the wiser one. Of course the object cf limit- ing the glass has arisen from the idea that, as it is a rapid conductor of cold or heat, it makes the house hot in sum- mer and cold in winter. This may be and is undoubtedly true, but the advantages to be derived from the using of glass more freelyare so great that it is worth while seek- ing to obtain these advantages, and at the same time avoid the ill effects of either excessive heat or cold. That this can be done is proved by American experience, for in that country there are greater extremes than are to be found in Great Britain. We are, therefore, compelled to say that the custom which has been hitherto adopted in this country is a wrong one, and to urge that there be given a much larger amount of window space in our poultry-houses. At the same time it is necessary to state that this must be done in the proper manner, or more harm than good will be the re- sult. One window should face the east, so placed as to catch :the early morning rays of the sun, and another may be placed on the west side for the purpose of re- ceiving the last glimpses of old Sol, but the principal window should be to the south, and the latter may be considerably the larger of the three. The east and west windows should be placed rather high so as to get the rays of the sun to the fullest extent. It is desirable that one or more of these windows be made to open, which one depending upon the place where the house is used. It is customary on the part of writers upon poultry.. keeping to say that the windows should always open on the south side of the house. But this would be the very worst advice that could be given for some places. The first time we ever visited a poultry establishment in the south-west district of England we were considerably astonished to see the houses facing the north. On inquiring the reason for this it was stated that there the winds troubling most of all were those from the south-west, Le., from the Atlantic, and it was necessary to have the house facing in the opposite direction. The same end could have been secured if the highest side of the houses had been made to the north, the opening window to the east, and the principal window opening to the south, for in that case all the benefit of the sun- light would have been secured, without any more expo- sure to the winds. From this it will be seen that the arrangement of the house must be made to suit the con- ditions under which it is placed. We are, however, thoroughly of the opinion that the American system is the better of tte two. But in order to overcome the rapid conduct of heat and cold it is necessary to use either very thick plate glass, or, what is much better, a double thickness of the ordinary window glass, leaving a space between the two. The best windows for poultry. houses are the sashes used in dwelling-houses. These are rather more costly, but the money will be well spent. In all poultry houses it is necessary to have one large door for the use of the attendant, and a small trap door for the exit of the fowls. The position of both must in large measure depend upon the position where the house is placed. It is, however, desirable under all circum- stances to have them where the inmates will not be un- duly exposed to cold or draught, for if put on the windy or cold side of the house it will scarcely be possible to keep the house comfortable. For instance, where we reside, the east winds are the most troublesome, and it is simply impossible to maintain the comfort of a room in the dwelling-house whose window faces east. And in the poultry houses, which are not so substantial, where either an opening window or door looks east, the inmates are .miserable when the wind is in that quarter. All, therefore, that need be said is that neither the large door, or the small trap, or an opening window should be on the windy side of the house. The prevention of this is not difficult. It is better when a shed is attached to the roosting place to permit the trap to open therein, both for protection and for the convenience of the fowls. This latter should be a foot wide and 18in. high, except for the very largest breeds, when it may be din. wider and 3in. higher. It should be covered with a sliding trap, and if there is any danger of robbers some provi- sion should be made so that the latter can be fastened on the inside. Two feet six inches is the usual width for the larger door, and the better it is fitted the more pro- tection will there be against unwelcome draughts. What material the house shall be built of depends so much upon the local conditions and circumstances that it is scarcely possible to recommend that which will suit all readers. Where the poultry-keeper is landowner also, or has a certain tenure, the best thing to go in for is stone or brick, if either be available, for they will be found the cheapest in the long run. A well-built poultry- house has very much to do with the success of the ven- ture. Brick and stone are both warmer than wood and do not need so much attention when erected. They should be plastered out to complete the matter, and kept well limewashed. But in many places, either because wood is much the cheapest, or for other reasons, this latter material is preferred, and, of course, for movable poultry-houses it must always be used. The general mistake made is in having the deals too thin. We have always used tongued flooring deals an inch thick, and a house so made and Well put together will be very warm and comfortable, quite enough for all ordinary require- ments. The advantage of using the tongued boards is that they are less liable to allow of interstices for the entrance of air or water. The roof can be made of various materials. On a brick or stone erection slates or tiles will look best, but they are rather expensive. They, of course, last well. Corru- gated galvanised iron sheeting has come into use very much of late years for 'poultry-houses, and it is cheap, handy, and lasts well. But it is a very rapid conductor of heat and cold, and when used the inside of the roof must be lined out with wood, or the fowls will be either roasted or starved in accordance with the season of the year. Wood makes a good roof, but will not answer alone, and it must either be covered with felting, with Willesden paper, or be well tarred and sanded.:Ne have sometimes made a very cheap roof covering. and also used the same for the sides of wooden houses, by first tarring the wood and then while it was wet layir'y, on sheets of brown paper, tarring the whole over again two or three times. This, if each coat is allowed to dry be- fore the next is put on, makes a splendid covering. Not the least important part of a poultry-house is the floor. If this be not properly made, no matter how well done the rest of the house is, it cannot be right. A damp florr me tns a damp house. There is also another con- sideration. If the house floor be not capable of being 'kept sweet then the atmosphere of the house can never be pure. This is a point upon which many poultry- houses entirely fail. In process of time the floor be- comes charged with ammonia from the droppings, and this impregnates the air day and night. What wonder then if the fowls do not thrive, and take all manner of diseases unaccountably. The floor we like best of all is sand, either from the sea shore or a .pit, but this is not available in all places. Wherever it can be used it should be. The floor is better dug out to the depth of eighteen inches, and half filled in with coarse gravel, or burnt brick ballast, or small stones, well beaten down. Above the sand will be placed, and it can be raked over daily, and renewed every six months, or whenever needed. Failing this the best floor is made by having the layer below as already stated, but instead of the sand a compost should be prepared of cinder ashes, fine gravel, quicklime, and water, well mixed together, and spread over. When hardened this makes a first class floor. Cement is far too cold, and bricks absorb the moisture from the droppings, so that neither of these materials should be used. It is desirable that the floor inside the house be higher than the ground without, for if lower it will certainly be damp.
